speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. W. A. BOYS (South Simcoe) present ed the .following report of the Special Committee to whom was referred Bill No. 14 to amend the Indian Act:
1.	Your committee convened on the 31st day of March, 1920, and thereafter held seventeen meetings, hearing thirty-five Indian witnesses from various parts of Canada, and in addition heard long and able addresses from three counsel learned in the law who appeared for the Six Nation Indians and certain of the Allied Tribes of British Columbia.
2.	Having given Bill No. 14 careful consideration, your committee have agreed to report the same with amendments, and for the information of the House report herewith their minutes of evidence and the exhibits filed in connection therewith.
3.	That in the opinion of your committee the administration of the affairs of an Indian community or band by an hereditary council may be detrimental to the best interests and progress of such Indians, and your committee would therefore recommend that wherever such a system exists the Government should ascertain whether the majority of the male members of the band of the full age of twenty-one years, are in favour of the adoption of an elective system of councillors, and if so, that the provisions of the Indian Act in this regard should be put into operation as soon as possible.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
4.	During the meetings held by your committee many of the Indian Chiefs expressed great satisfaction with the opportunity the meetings gave them of presenting their views to a Committee of Parliament, and many intimated that if this opportunity was given more frequently it would lead to a better understanding of Indian Affairs, and having in view the strong representations made in this connection, your committee would recommend that the rules of the House be amended to provide for the appointment of a Select Standing Committee upon Indian Affairs.
5.	Your committee therefore commend the suggestions contained in paragraphs 3 and 4 hereof to the favourable consideration of the Government.
All which is respectfully submitted.
Signed W. A. Boys, Chairman.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, I move thait the -House do this day resolve itself into 'Committee of the Whole to consider the resolution standing in his name to amend the Customs Act.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Motion agreed to.

On m-otion of right ho®. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) the House w-ent into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Customs Act, and to provide that the Governor in Council may from time to time make regulations for or relating to the exportation of any article, commodity or material which is produced or manufactured in Canada, and which is, in the opinion of the Governor in Council, necessary or desirable for the use -or consumption of the Canadian people, or for the encouragement, maintenance or preservation of any trade, industry, business or occupation, and may by such regulations order and direct that any such article, commodity or material shall be exported only under license issued by the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, or by an officer appointed upon the minister's recommendation for that purpose; and that the issue of any such license, and the exercise of any right or privilege thereby conferred, shall be subject to such conditions as the Governor in Council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue shall prescribe;
That every such regulation shall have force and effect after it has been published in the Canada Giazette, and that it shall be laid before Parliament within fifteen days after the date thereof if Parliament is then dn session and, if not, within the first fifteen days of the session held next after the date thereof, and shall remain in force until the day immediately succeeding the day of prorogation of that session of -Parliament and no longer-, unless during that session it be approved by resolution of both Houses of Parliament; and
That any person violating any provision of any such regulation shall be liable upon summary conviction to a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars for each violation.
He said: This is an important resolution. I am asking the House to go into committee on- it now so that I may introduce the Bill. After the Bill has been introduced, and if i-t -receives the approval of the House upon its second reading, I shall move that it be referred -to -a -Select Committee of the House before it is taken up in Committee of the Whole. I have -spoken to my hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and also to the member for Marquette (Mr. Urerar), suggesting thait that course be followed. I should like to have -the resolution- adopted, if the committee approves, pro -forma, with, of course, full liberty of discussion when the Bill is taken up in Committee of the Whole after it has been considered by Ithe -Special -Committee to which I have referred.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext: To my mind this is the most important piece of legislation that has been brought before Parliament this session. Generally, restrictions upon importation have been regarded as,-well, I might even use the word immoral; they are such a restraint of trade that people will not put up with them. Under the constitution of the United States restricted importation was forbidden. Of course, we shall have to go into the matter, but it seems to me that this proposed legislation will require a good deal of explanation on the part of the Government. For my part, I would like to know of some concrete cases in connection with which legislation of this kind becomes necessary in time of peace and under ordinary conditions. We complain that we have a large debt; that our currency is at a discount; that the balance of trade is against us. Now we are going to place in the hands of the Govern-jmenb the power to neisfadct exports of any kind of commodity. Whatever the reason may be, I do not think that there is any emergency to call for action of that kind. Unless the special committee submit a report on the matter which changes my mind, I shall be absolutely and entirely opposed to vesting any such power in the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext:
Perhaps my
hon. friend is not alive to the situation that confronts the country at the present time. Important and very urgent representations have been made to the Government as to the necessity of some control of export in respect to important articles. For example, we are told that a large amount of coal is going out of the country while industries are suffering through lack of it. The item of sugar is also under consideration; the necessity for some action in that .regard has been strongly urged upon us. Then, there is the question of newsprint. .Urgent representations have been made from different parts of the country that because of the exportation of an amount not exceeding two per cent of the exportable surplus, the shutting down of some twenty-seven Canadian newspapers is involved.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext: I understood that it was fifteen per cent of the production.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext: I am informed that only two per cent of the total exportable surplus of that particular article is involved in the question. The Governor in Council has no desire to assume burdens or responsibilities in this respect. I hope .that the special committee to whom this Bill will be referred will find some means of relieving the Governor in Council from a duty which involves great responsibility and is wholly invidious. No one would be more delighted than I if that committee .could find some effective method which .will meet the conditions of public urgency now confronting the country and at the same time relieve the Government from additional responsibility. All I ask, however, at the present moment is that the matter may be expedited by passing the .resolution pro forma, and upon the second reading or in committee the House will be ,at liberty to decide whether or not this legislation or any legislation of an analogous character ought to be passed by this House, or whether we should allow matters to take the course they are now taking.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext:
There are abundant
reasons why it would not be advisable for us to have a protracted discussion at the present time, although there are some matters which we. might well consider before we come to a conclusion. Therefore, I trust it will be the view of the committee that, without committing ourselves to the principle of the resolution we should now allow the resolution to pass the present stage.

Mr. MoMASTER: I should be sorry to disagree with or to fail to follow any arrangement made by the leader of the party to which I belong, but this proposed legislation is to my mind so vicious that I wish to have an opportunity given on the introduction of the resolution of speaking to it. It would be very well for the country to be fully advised as to what the Government purpose doing. I would have thought that the Canadian nation was thoroughly sick of the Government endeavouring to control industry, and it is surely bad enough to have a protectionist government in power with the right to control imparts into the country, but it would be worse to have them control exports from the country. I should like, if that could be agreed to by all, to have a general discussion on the introduction of this resolution. We cannot canvass the situation too fully, and now is the time to do it. If what is proposed to be done is done, it means that the matter goes to a committee and that it will not get back into this House until the middle of next week. We are hopeful of being able to bring the session to a termination before Dominion Day. What will happen if we do not have this discussion now will be that if this legislation is passed, it will have tea be rushed through in the dying hours of the session. I protest most respectfully against that line of conduct, and I would ask that the rules of the House be adhered to and a discussion take place.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.
speechtext: I am not asking for any departure from the rules of the House. The purpose that I have in view is one that should meet entirely the view of the hon. gentleman. It is highly probable, in fact, practically certain that the measure to which the House will eventually be .asked to give its assent, will differ in important respects from that which is embodied ;n this resolution, and for the reason that I want the House to have full opportunity of discussion, I am endeavouring now to advance the proceedings in order that the measure may be referred to the proposed committee and be reported upon as soon as possible, so that the hon. gentleman and those who concur in his view may have the full opportunity of debating it which all of us desire.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.

Might I say to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) that I think he misunderstands the remarks which the Prime Minister (.Sir Robert Borden) made a moment ago when

he interprets them as meaning that there had been any arrangement or understanding between the Prime Minister and myself in regard to this matter? The Prime Minister, as he stated this afternoon, informed me that in connection with this resolution there were certain matters which he believed could be more expeditiously and carefully dealt with toy a committee representative of both sides of the House, and that we would make more progress with what may be proposed in the way of legislation, through considering the matter in special committee and having a report for the House to act upon, rather than by having a general discussion which might range very far beyond the purpose of this resolution. When the Prime Minister spoke to me in those words, I thought the course he was suggesting was in the interest of expediting the business of the House .and that it was the part of wisdom not to bring up in this House for discussion many subjects that, perhaps, might be construed as coming within the scope of the resolution, but which, if it went to a committee, would be eliminated. There has been no understanding. I feel, however, in view of what the Prime Minister has said in the House today, which is exactly what he said to me privately, that the course which the Prime Minister has suggested is a wise course to pursue.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT-RESOLUTION RESPECTING PROPOSED EXPORT REGULATIONS.

Any", u"man who bad attained to any one of these offices might be considered a great man; but the man who has attained to all of them is,, in my judgment, indeed a great man. I venture to submit with all due respect to the hon. and gallant member for Victoria, that he ought not from his place in the House to have referred to General Sir Arthur Currie as he did to-day, knowing quite we'll that what he said would go out through the press to the country as a .statement seriously reflecting upon Sir Arthur Currie as a general and a gentleman.
I served1 under Sir Arthur Currie for some two years, and I .served with him for some two years more. I found hiim to be a man of character,-and character is the supreme military virtue. He was an honest man, a just man, and a fair man. I neve- heard him refer to any officer or soldier in terms suggestive of any personal animosity, and yet I have known him on occasion to be severe and, I think, justly and properly severe. He was a great tactician and a great strategist. Upon all occasion\xae he displayed the greatest concern in regard to the future movements of troops, and no man grieved more sincerely over the losses we .suffered than did General Sir Arthur Currie.
I have said that he was a great strategist and a great tactician-in a word, a great general. In saying that I am stating the opinion of those who .served under him and who were competent to express an opinion, and I am also stating the opinion of distinguished generals and leaders in the Allied Armies, all of whom have placed on record their opinion that Sir Arthur Currie was a great leader and a great soldier.
The hon. and gallant member for Victoria has referred to a propaganda in support of the assertion that Sir Arthur Currie w.as .a great general. I. am not aware of any such propaganda, nor am I aware that any such was necessary. On the other hand, I have been aware for some time that there has been a propaganda by assertions made, .covertly and indirectly, to make it appear that Sir Arthur Currie in the pursuit of his own glory sacrificed his men,- that many men might have been alive to-day but for the desire of General Sir Arthur Currie to obtain some personal distinction. I say that there has been a propaganda to that effect, and it has been supported and carried on by those not competent to have any sound opinion upon the question. It has been a very cruel and unjust form o>f propaganda, because it has not only interfMr. Grlesbach.]
ested those who are more or less casual observers; it has touched the heartstrings of those who have suffered personally in this war in the loss of those who were near and dear to them. I say it was an unkind and ungenerous propaganda, and I regret that the hon. and gallant member for Victoria (Sir -Sam Hughes) has had his share in that propaganda in this House and without this House. As an old comrade, one who had the most complete opportunity of studying and of measuring General Currie as a soldier and as a man, I should like to say that in my humble opinion he is a great Canadian and a great soldier, and that he deserves well of this country.

There is an

In the grain business, for example, the custom is to give a demand note showing the exact amount of advances each day. The usual period of credit is three months, and if the two cents were to be charged on every hundred dollars of each note each day there would be a multiplication of the tax, although noit of credit. iSome of the elevator companies have shown that transactions often involve a balance of from five to six millions dollars at the end of the day's work, and that there may be changes resulting from sales cutting that down probably a million or a million and a half, while there may be further obligations resulting from purchases which might increase it a million or a million and a half or two millions. But the note for the whole amount is taken in each instance. It is proposed to modify that in the Bill. Then, in order properly to cover the question, it is also necessary to place a similar tax on advances made by banks hy way of overdraft. Such advances are probably the most unsatisfactory method by which the banking

business can be carried on, and it is the only way in which an advance is not evidenced, as it should be evidenced, by the signature of the debtor. Advances by way of overdraft are entirely illegal in the United States. It is not proposed here to make them so at the present time, but simply to make the credit which is obtained by the advance subject to the same two cent stamp tax as the credit given by the promissory note is subject to.

speechtext: The injustice of the process is this: If I give a note at thirty or ninety days and pay my two cents on it, I owe the bank for a definite period. As a rule their proprietors cannot afford to pay for one of the more expensive feature films, and therefore they have to run (more films than the better class of movie theatres, often showing 6 to 8 films each day. speechtext: I really think the minister did not pay sufficient attention to the suggestion tmalde by my hbn. friend (Mr. Fielding) llast night in regard tto bagpipes. maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
May I sum tbis up as I understand it? What has been paid under resolutions which have really never become law is going to remain the loss of the man who has bought goods and paid the tax. There was no authority and there never has been any authority to collect this tax. These resolutions were presented to Parliament, but tbis legislation is valid only inasmuch as and when the Bill is assented to. When the Bill is assented to, what is in the Bill is law. My English is limited, but I might say that it is not within the dignity of Parliament to act in this way, namely, to make temporary measures, and then when Parliament in its wisdom has discussed them, to say to the public: Gentlemen, we have brought down measures that we do not think it proper to have on the Statute Book; it was not wise on our part to enact such legislation; but we are going to penalize you on that legislation which was proposed but which is not in force. We are,' in effect, saying to the public:	Those who
bought the goods within the period and paid the tax will pay* the penalty and suffer the loss, and those who did not buy the goods within the period will not have to suffer any loss. I know it is hard to have to reimburse people; but those who have overpaid ought to be reimbursed; there

ought to be a refund. I do not think, as a Parliament, we are giving a proper example, when we say to people:	Although
we have made a mistake in not coming *down to Parliament with proper legislation, we are going to have you pay for that and we are not going to make a refund. As regards the new resolutions, if the amounts that have been paid should have been greater, well and good, put on the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: That would be making the new resolutions retroactive.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend will not contend that, as regards these new regulations there are any duties to-day in .force. This legislation will be in force .when it passes the Senate and is assented to by the Governor General. This is retroactive, corresponding with the statement made in the House; but it is not a law; it is only a Bill. Supposing the Bill should go no further, how could it be enforced? I do not think the Senate could throw out the Bill, because it is a matter of the exchequer; but supposing it should be voted down, what would happen? The point of ,the matter is that there is no absolute certainty of this becoming law; it becomes law only when the Governor General has assented to the Bill, and it is practically, to all intents and purposes, retroactive, because it will date back to the 19th May. To-day, the 16th June, we are making this .amendment; but there is no law in fact, .there is nothing to compel a man to pay the tax until we ratify these resolutions. .Therefore, we have collected something which we have no right to collect, but still we are making this valid from the day it .is assented to by the Governor General. In my opinion, this is acquiescing in legislation which in itself is unjust.
v Mr. DENIS:	Unwise.
, Mr. BUREAU: This is not a question of wisdom. It is unjust, but I should like to use a stronger word than that,

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Iniquitous.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: No, it is not iniquitous, but it is very close to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I	confess I
have not had time to * go over the authorities, but I would ask my hon. friend to turn to a few of them, about which he probably knows a great deal more than I do. I am told that what is now done always has been done whenever changes are made,
[.Mr. Bureau.]
,and that in some instances very radical .changes have been made. I speak subject ,to correction because I have not had time ,to turn up Hansard, but I am told that exactly the same course was taken in 1896, .and in the session of 1897, when radical .changes were made in the Budget. I am .told that this is the course invariably followed in England. Again, I speak subject to correction; but I know that it is .the universal custom for Budget proposals to take effect the very moment they are .announced. Moreover, I am sure that my hon. friend will appreciate this, that whatever he may think as regards the question of principle, which apparently all British .Parliaments have followed, it is absolutely impracticable to apply a system of rebates, .particularly when you have many small .taxes paid by people nobody knows who .they are, nobody can tell who they may ,be. Just see the position my hon. friend ,would put the retailer in if this resolution .was not passed. Whatever we may say as ,to the theoretical position, fortified by any .kind of language my hon. friend cares to use in characterizing it, the fact still remains that Budget resolutions have always .taken effect when brought down. It is .absolutely impracticable to give refunds in connection with a series of small taxes like these. The very people who have been objecting to these taxes, that is the merchants, would be placed in an impossible position if refunds were ordered. The situation is taken care of in the same way as it .has been taken care of in the past. We cannot escape from that.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
May I draw the minister's attention to the difference between this Budget and previous Budgets? Previous Budgets dealt with customs duties on articles imported into Canada and with excise duties. If the people knew beforehand that new taixee were coming into effect there would be wild speculation. For instance, if it wias known that .a tax of $2 a gallon would be imposed on whisky, the distilleries would be run dry before the tax caim-e into effect. But this Budget is different. This Budget taxes the individual because he uses a -certain article. You might say that that is also true of whisky, hut it is only the man who drinks the whisky who pays the duty, and if th-e resolutions were net brought into effect immediately he would 'take advantage of the situation and Speculate. UndeT this Budget it is the consumer that pays -the tax, and we had no right ait the time he paid ithe tax to make him pay it. For instance, suppose

a man has paid a $2 tax on shoes and the exemption price has since been changed. The Government is going to get the benefit of that 'tax. I say that ils robbing the people; it is taking money which we have absolutely no right to take. I say the principle is wrong, and I toaite to acquiesce in it, and I do not think I shall.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The principle is the same in both cases; it only differs in degree. A man malkes a raid on the whisky 'Seller for the purpose of saving $2 a gallon. I do not see why he should not stock himself up with boots in order to save an extra $2 a pair.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: There are eight million people affected by these taxes, but only one or two hundred would speculate in whisky.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend puts it thait way his case is all the weaker, because only one hundred would make a raid on whisky while there aire eight million to mlake a raid on booth.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: To make the matter perfectly clear, would the minister say just when Ithe changes we iare now adopting, or have adopted, will come into force. Are they coming into force to-day when the resolutions are adopted by the committee, or 'when the Bill is introduced?

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

They will come into effect on the first reading of the Bill, which I have here ready for utbs first reading.

speechtext:
I wanted to say a word on behalf of the ordinary medicines that are dispensed in a drug store under prescription, This question was raised last night,
.a.nd the minister said he was willing to do something if some scheme could be worked out. I want to place myself on record *as opposed to this extra tax on alcohol, so far as 'the ordinary prescription medicine is concerned. A few prescriptions may be given that are not absolutely necessary, but generally speaking, when a doctor gives a prescription in any part, of this country it is for the purpose of curing illness. In many oases 'the patients who get that prescription may 'be able to pay any price for iit, but if a man as ill it does not matter whether he has money ot not, he has to be treated, and the medical profession of this country will treat him. If be is treated iat home the question of getting medicine is .an important one to the patient. A bottle of medicine that you could get on a doctor's prescription for something like 60 oents not very long ago now costs very much more 'than, that, and this extra tax on alcohol is going to run up the price on these prescription medicines very highly. I should say that it would run up liquid medicines in which tinctures are contained, and most bottles of medicine contain tinctures, perhaps' 25 or 30 and in some case even 50 per cent. I should like to impress on the minister the necessity of working out some scheme of drawback, or something of that kind, to the makers of these tinctures. It cannot be done for the druggists, of whom it has been stated there are over 3,000 in this country, hut you could give a drawback to the manufacturers of these tinctures who supply the druggists. While that would discriminate to a certain extent against the small manufacturer and the druggist who makes his own tinctures, I do not think there are many druggists making their own tinctures at the present time, and it would give a certain amount of retlief to ithe poor who require these prescriptions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I do not think that is a matter thait could be considered on the resolution before the House, but it could he considered in connection with the customs regulation's, on section 92, if I remember rightly, of the Audit Act. maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the minister to an inconsistency in one or two items of the resolutions. I would refer the minister to an item in paragraph (a) of resolution 1, reading as follows:	,

Kimonas, petticoats and waists in excess of $12 eaoh.
Then in the amended resolutions there is this item:
Silk clothing including artificial silk clothing not elsewhere specified.
Then a ruling given last night by the minister Teads (Hansard, p. 3693):
The tax applies on all silk manufactured garments whether they be overskirts or anything else.
That ruling means that all kinds of gar- [DOT] ments manufactured from silk are taxable.
I do not think there is any such article as petticoats or waist in excess of $12 that is not made of silk. There are silk waists that, cost less than -$12. and I therefore suggest that the section I have referred to be amended to read-
Petticoats and waists of silk and other materials, and kimonas in excess of $12.
I know that a silk waist is an article that is very much in use and it is not a luxury up to that price. If my amendment is adopted1 it will include all waists up to that price whether made of silk, georgette crepe or any other of the materials that are largely used at the present time in the manufacture of such garments. I trust that the minister will consider the representation I am making in this regard.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I am pleased to support the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Pedlow). We have taxed silk dresses and skirts and various other garments and I think we should make a small concession to the ladies and exempt waists.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If I am not in order in -moving this amendment now, I trust the minister will consider the .point I have raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I do not think the situation is quite as the hon. member conceives it. Silk 'clothing "not otherwise specified" is all taxable, font sometimes it is specified. Now kimonas, petticoats and waists are not excepted because they are generally made of silk. Silk garments generally if not specified are 'subject to the tax; if specified they are -made suibject to the excise tax; so that so far as kimonas, petticoats and waists are concerned they become taxable when the cost is over $12. Similarly silk stockings are specially dealt with.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I think it is absolutely necessary to revise the clause as I have suggested, to read: "petticoats and waists of silk and other materials and kimonas." That phraseology is necessary 'because ki-

monas may or may not be made of silk. As it is, there may he 'misunderstanding in construing the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I shall he glad to consider the point.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Last night the resolutions were amended so as to make it clear that cake was not confectionery and would not come under that classification. There are a number of things such as soup, which is a manufactured article, that are exempted; yet it is doubtful whether ordinary cake sold by the small baker will be totally exempt from the sales tax. Will the minister explain that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Cakes have been removed from the class of confectionery. But, not being an essential food, they should be .subject to the one per cent turnover. For example, the turn-over of the Christie Company will be subject to the 1 per cent when selling to the wholesaler; in the same way cakes will be subject to the turn-over tax.
Mr. .GLASS: I desire to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that was under discussion last night, namely, the question of containers. A firm in London who are manufacturing and shipping goods use a large amount of silicate of soda, which is shipped in large drums invoiced at $15 a piece. These drums come to the country being simply rented for the transportation of this substance which is used in this manufacturing business,' and they are returned to the company who own them. This manufacturing concern have to pay duty on these drums and they are advised by the Customs Department that if they can identify the drums and show that they are refilled and returned to them they will avoid paying duty on them a second time. It is absurd that a large organization having thousands of shipping containers sent all over the country should be expected to have, say, a hundred drums shipped to any point in 'Canada identified and marked and returned to be refilled. It is just as absurd to expect that as it is to expect that a large standard oil company could refill the same barrels and consign them to the same consignee a second and a third time. If the Bill does not provide some means of avoiding the duty the second time on these containers, I would suggest to the minister that he seriously consider the question of giving some relief from the charges that will be imposed on the manufacturer in that respect.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: I desire to ask the minister a question and he can answer the two at the same time. My question is in reference to gasoline drums or containers which are used in large quantities in the western provinces to take gasolene and kerosene to the farms for use in Gas Tractors. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: If they invoice them then they would be taxed. But it does not seem to me that they should invoice them. Only one set of containers should be in question, and it would be entirely wrong to pyramid costs on containers. Do they not give a refund on returning the containers?

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: When these drums are first taken out the customer is charged $15 apiece on them. That would make a tax of fifteen cents each at one per cent. If he takes ten drums in the first place and returns them at the end of one week, taking out another ten, there is no sale. It is merely an exchange of containers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: The fifteen cents ought to be refunded in each case in which it is charged.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: It is quite evident that there are a number of commodities that are left uncertain .and the merchants of the country are wondering what their rights are. All foods are exempt from the sales tax, but what would be the interpretation as to jellies and jams contained in bottles? Is baker's bread subject to the sales tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: So I understand but the object of my raising this question is to know hlow far this clause will be subject to the interpretation of the minister or of the department so that if people now have a doubt or a grievance it may be considered or removed later on. Will the minister make a statement which will be re-assuring to those who are at present in doubt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
This is a point which certainly Ought to be covered and the
Bill ought to have some provision which would enable all doubts to be set at rest and all questions toi be settled in pursuance of the principles laid down. There is no difficulty about canned goods or jellies and jams in bottles. The one is a cheap form of food not subject to the tax but jellies and jams in bottles are what are known as pound goods containing a great quantity of sugar and it is not the intention to exempt them from the tax.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I would like to emphasize the point I made a moment ago in regard to containers, and in that connection I desire to read a letter which was sent by the Commissioner of Customs on Miay 20, 1920, to the London Shipping Containers, Limited. These people import silicate of soda which they use in manufacturing certain containers. These containers in which they import the silicate of soda are rented to them at $15 each. They come in, they pay the duty of 30 per cent on this $15 and then the containers are .returned to the United States and the London firm are credited with the full price charged. The firm asked for a refund of the duty on these containers and this is the letter of the Commissioner of Customs dated 20th May last:
Ottawa, May. 26th, 1920. Messrs. London Shipping Containers, Limited, London, Ontario.
Attention R. L. Stephenson Esq.,
Manager.
Gentlemen:-
Subject:

Return of metal drums free of duty after duty has once been paid.
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your favour of the 15th instant enclosing a contract which you have with the Philadelphia Quartz Company in connection with the purchase of Silicate of Soda. This Soda is put up in metal drums holding approximately 1,400 lbs., and you are asked to pay a duty of 30 per cent on these drums on each importation. Tou state that if these drums1 are marked for exportation, it is impossible to -have these identical drums returned to you as the exporters, the Philadelphia Quartz Company have about 5,000 of these drums.
Tou are advised in reply that if the identical drums which have been marked on exportation for identification are not returned, there is no authority under the Customs regulations for allowing free entry of the same as provided for in memorandum No. 1398-B, copy of which I enclose.
I have the honour to be Gentlemen,
Tours obedient servant, Acting Commissioner of Customs.
If the customs laws of this country provide so. absurd and unreasonable a condi-

tion to toe applied to an importer, I submit this is the time and the place to change so unjust a provision. Sometimes the rulings of the Customs Department are unjustly made because there is no such ambiguity in the laws that they do not know what they mean. They have to have another Act to interpret the original Act, and even then it is difficult to know what the law means. This substance which is dealt with in this letter is a necessary article in process of manufacture, and if the duty is paid on the drums once and the drums are returned, surely these people ought not to be asked to pay duty again on the same drums. I submit that the request is a reasonable one and that this grievance should be adjusted right here while Parliament is in session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I have so many troubles of my own that I am reluctant to take up any customs matter. We have no resolutions dealing with the customs tariff. We are not considering customs regulations1, or the customs tariff. The question with regard to drum containers is a very vexed one which has been going on for many years. I confess I do not know enough about it to enable me to answer my hon. friend. This is a tax on turn-over and on the net turn-over at that. What I might -suggest is that a refund be given for each and every holder or drum which is sent forward and which is returned. We could not fairly treat drums as forming a part of the produce under the circumstances and they will not be so treated.

speechtext: On the motion for Committee of Supply:

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Militia and Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I would like to make a few preliminary observations on the Estimates submitted by the Department of Militia and Defence. I do so particularly because I think there exists not only in the country, but in the press and within the House of Commons some misapprehension as to the scope of the proposals which I have the honour now to bring before the House.
It has been a matter of some criticism during the present session that apparently the amount of the militia Estimates submitted this year is largely in excess of the amount submitted for the last fiscal year. On more than one occasion comparisons have been made between the figure now submitted-in round numbers, $12,500,000 -and the amount submitted last year-in round numbers, $8,369,000. The statement has been made that it is proposed to expend during the coming year about $4,000,000 more for Militia and Defence than was found necessary last year and an argument has been based upon the comparison that the Government is entering upon a career of recklessness in regard to militia expenditure. But I submit that no fair or proper comparison can be made between the amount submitted this year and the amount submitted last year, for very obvious reasons. Any one who takes time to consider the situation as we have it to-day and the situation as we had it last year must at once, I think, realize the force of what I say. Last year was a war year in this country and was so treated by this Parliament. This year, technically speaking, is perhaps a war year too, but not to the same

extent as was last year, and so far as possible during the present year we are trying to get back to normal affairs and the expenditure now submitted would be the expenditure of a normal year, not of a war year. In our militia expenditure we treated last year as a war year, and for that reason the expenditure appears at only about $8,391,000, but that does not mean that the sum of $8,391,000 was the total militia expenditure. The truth is that all sums of money expended last year which could be charged to War Appropriation were so charged, and the House knows that last year we appropriated $300,000,000 as a War Appropriation. This year the War Appropriation for expenditures both in this country and in Great Britain, where we are winding up war matters, is about $38,000,000. One has only to cast one's eye over the militia Estimates for the present year to see the difference between the proposed expenditure of this year and the expenditure of last year. In that expenditure there are eight items which show increases during the present year over last year, and these eight particular items to which I will call the attention of the House, account for almost $4,000,000 of the increase.
The first item which shows an increase in this years proposal is that of annual drill. Last year annual drill appeared only at the sum of $350,000; as a matter of fact, while there was no annual drill last year except by the permanent forces of Canada, the ordinary militia units were not called on to drill. This year, at the time when these Estimates were prepared and printed, it was expected that the usual annual drill would take place throughout Canada; that is, the drill which we were accustomed to have in this country before the war in normal times. If the committee will look at the item for the year 1913-14, as shown at page 30 of the Estimates, they will see that in the year before the war the item for annual drill was $1,830,000. This year it was estimated that a sum of $1,500,000 would suffice for the item of annual drill, on the .assumption that the ordinary militia units would be sufficiently organized to perform annual drill during the present summer. I may, however, tell the committee at this juncture that our hopes in that respect ,have been somewhat disappointed. The organization or re-organization of the militia units in this country has not proceeded sufficiently far to enable us to go ahead with the ordinary annual drill. Annual drill this year will be confined to what are known as city

corps who can train at their local headquarters; but the organization of the rural units which perform annual drill in the month of June throughout Canada has not proceeded far enough, and their annual drill will have to be abandoned for the present year, although the permanent force will drill as usual. The item, however, as it appears in the Estimates was for the old time programme of annual drill as it was held in this country prior to the war. There is a difference in that item between this year and last year of $1,150,000. That cannot be regarded as an extravagance; if we are to maintain in Canada a militia force, it must be a drilled force, a competent force, and the item for annual drill should appear in the Estimates, although, as I stated, this year the annual drill will not take place because organization has not proceeded far enough to permit of that.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: What will the reduction amount to?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
As regards annual drill of rural troops, the reduction will be approximately $400,000. The only authority we have given so far is for annual drill to be performed by city corps. The estimate of the number of men who make up city battalions which will drill at local headquarters is about 30,000 in round figures. In addition to that we hope to train such of our batteries of artillery as have local headquarters where they can be trained. There are seven or eight or nine thousand of these men who may be trained, and in addition to that we are going to make an effort to train our new machine gun units established for the first time in this country, no doubt as an outcome of the Great War. These will be all the troops that will be trained in addition to the training which is going on at the present time of the permanent force. If the city units and batteries of artillery and machine gun units are trained at local headquarters, as we propose, there will be a saving on this item alone of approximately $400,000. There will, I think, be a greater saving than that, but I am giving that as the estimated amount.
Another item that will bear comparison between this year and last is that of cadet services. The amount for cadet services this year is placed at $390,000, while before the war the amount was $392,500. Last year the amount dropped down to $100,000, bo that there is an apparent increase this year over last year of $290,000. Last year was a war year; we were trying to keep militia expenditure in this country as low as possible; last year we had no cadet camps. This year we purpose holding the ordinary cadet
camps which did so much for the military service of this country in years gone by. Last year there was no military class, no physical training class for the teachers in the cadet corps. This year we propose to re-establish those as heretofore. Last year there was no grant for uniforms for cadet corps. The grant is not large, something about one dollar per man, and this year we purpose giving these grants again. That acounts for the difference of $290,000 shown in the Estimates, but there is this to be said of this item. I am informed by those who are most competent in this country to advise one upon such a point that the most valuable asset we have from a militia point of view is our cadet training, and that for the future, perhaps for all time to come, the most valuable class of people to whom we can look in this country to form our militia is the school children of to-day. We have not established anything in the nature of compulsory military training; we give them a plain course of physical instruction, a .course which improves the lad both in body and in mind, if he never subsequently enters the militia. But, as a matter of fact, that preliminary training has had a great deal to do with filling up our militia units throughout the country. This is a most valuable expenditure if we are to maintain a militia force in Canada.
The next item is that of Dominion arsenals, which this year shows an expenditure of $790,000 at Lindsay and Quebec. Last year no expenditure whatever was shown for this item. Last year we had a very heavy expenditure, but* it was charged to War Appropriation, so that the expenditure this year appears as an increase, although, as a matter of fact, it is not an increase at all.
The next item that shows an increase between last year and this year is that of engineer services, and there is an apparent increase in that item of $230,000. That is really not an increase. Last year the work was not fully performed; our military establishments, barracks, buildings and the like were not kept up as they should have been, but what work was done while these buildings were being occupied by the Canadian Expeditionary troops was charged to War Appropriation. This year we do not purpose charging it to Demobilization Appropriation, but to the appropriation which now appears in the Estimates under this heading of engineer services.
The next item is for the permanent force, which shows an increase of $428,000 over last year. That item I will deal with in the

course of a few minutes. The next is Transport and Freight, which shows an increase over last year of $275,000. Last year the expenditure under that head was $25,000, and I do not think it was spent. There was no transport and there was no freight, because there was no training and there were no camps. All the military transport which took place in Canada last year was charged to War Appropriation; it had strictly to do with the war, and not with the established militia of this country. Now that we are getting hack to normal times this item is charged to the Militia vote. We do not expect to use the whole of it because a large part of it would ordinarily be used in connection with the annual camps, and as we are not going to drill rural battalions, there will be a considerable saving in that item. The item is about the same as in normal years before the war, allowing for the increases in freight and passenger rates which have taken place in the interval,
The next item is Warlike Stores. There is an apparent increase there of $400,060 over last year. Last year there was no separate expenditure under this head. All expenditure on warlike stores last year was charged to War Appropriation.
In the eight items I have enumerated there is in the aggregate an apparent increase of $3,700,000, but I think the House will agree that the increases are only apparent, not real increases. They are charged this year to the vote of the Militia Department. While last year for the most part they were charged to the War Appropriation. What I maintain is that a comparison between the proposals of this year and the proposals of last year is <nrt a fair comparison at all. A fair comparison would be to compare what we propose to spend this year, as a peace year, with what we spent in the year before the war, also a peace year. I am quite prepared to compare our expenditure, of this year with the expenditure in the year 1913-14, or in any of the four or five years before that, and justify the figures I now submit as reasonable and proper under the circumstances. Let us go back a few years before the war to the days of the Liberal administration.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Your administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The administration of which I was a humble supporter. I submit that the figures I now present compare favourably with the expenditure in those years. I go back to the year 1910-11, when the late Sir Frederick Borden presided over the Militia Department, and take the Es-

timates of that year, at page 47. The Main Estimates totalled-I shall give only round figures - $6,898,000, and the supplementar-ies, of which there were three, $236,000. .The total appropriation for that year was .$7,135,000. Coming to the year 1912, page 48 of the Estimates of that year, the Main Estimates of that year totalled $7,524,000. There were again three Supplementary Estimates of $56,870,	$463,000 and $155,000.
.The total for 1912 was $8,200,000. That was the Estimate for 1912, prepared in the year 1911. Now I come to the year 1913-14, .the figures for which are shown in the first .column of the Estimates now before us.
, Mr. LEMIEUX:	Would my hon. friend
supplement his statement by giving the figures of the national debt in those years?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
I cannot offhand, but
later I can give nay hon. friend that information if he desires it.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
We had money then;
,we have none now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
In 1913-14, the year immediately before the war, the Estimates totalled $10,917,000. But that year there were other military expenditures. One charged to Public Works amounted to $221,000, and other special expenditures for military purposes, as set out in the accounts, amounted to $740,000. The total for that year was $11,79,000. During the years 1911 and 1912 (our military establishment 'in panada was not very different from what it is to-day. The permanent force was very similar to the permanent force of today. In the year 1911-12 the permanent force of Canada consisted of 2,916 men of all ranks, and in 1913-14, the year before .the war, of 2,906 men of all ranks. The permanent force which exists in Canada at this date consists of exactly 3,555 men. |That is the total permanent force of the .'military establishment of this country. That is. we have in round numbers 555 more men of all ranks than we had the year before the war, or more than we had when Bir Frederick Borden brought in his Estimates in the year 1910-11.
Why should there be an increase shown .in the vote if the establishment is about the same? I think the reason is apparent to every member of the House. The cost ,of maintenance to-day is just about double ,what it was in those years. I have made inquiries and I find that the cost of food has more than doubled. I saw in the newspaper to-day a statement by the Department of Labour giving statistics. It showed that the cost of the weekly budget for a

family of five people increased from $7.45 in May 1914 to $16.65, or an increase of 125 per cent. The increase has been just as great in the cost of soldiers' food as in .the food of other people. Clothing has increased over 100 per cent. Ammunition and military equipment has increased on the the average by 100 per cent. Freight transport has increased about 75 per cent. Going ,up and down the whole line of figures, from .the best information I can gather from very competent men in the department to assist me in such matters, I find that the average increase has been between 80 and 90 per cent. Pay has been increased very much since Sir Frederick Borden's time, and very much since the year 1913-14. Taking the pay of a private only, in the year 1910-11 a private in the permanent force received 50 cents a day, after three years, 60 cents, and after six years, 75 cents. In 1912 this was changed a little. It .was made 50 cents on joining, 60 cents after three years, and 70 cents instead of 75 cents, after six years, but a small annual .allowance called an efficiency allowance was added, bringing the maximum pay of a private up to 90 cents a day. So it was ,at the outbreak of the war. We then established a new rate of pay for our soldiers. The pay -of a private in the expeditionary force was raised to $1.10 a day. Last year with the authority of Parliament that pay .was again increased. The new pay regulations provide that a private in the permanent force shall receive $1.70 a day, which is $51 a month, as against the 50 cents a day which he received	in	1910-11, and as against
50 cents and an efficiency allowance which he received the year previous to the war. ,The pay of all ranks has likewise been Increased, but not so much as the private's .pay. The last increase in the pay*of privates and non-commissioned officers constituted an average increase of 26 per cent, ,and the pay of officers has been increased about 10 per cent.
Any one can see the great difference between the 50 cent pay which pertained in our permanent force eight or ten years ago and the $1.70 which pertains to-day or the' $1.10 which was paid throughout the war. These matters make up the whole of this increase,-100 per cent in pay and 100 per cent in equipment, and all food and clothing double what it was formerly. Now, while the permanent force has only been increased by 555 men of all ranks during these intervening years, are the figures which we show to-day in any respect un-231

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: reasonable? I submit that they are not. There is a popular impression in Canada that in some way this Government has increased the military establishment of the country.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
Let me deal with that
supposition for a moment. My hon. friend from Laprairie says "hear, hear." I know he has not the correct information on the subject and I will give it to him now, because the fact is that the militia and the permanent forces have not been materially increased. Twelve years ago, indeed longer than that, in 1903 or 1904, Parliament authorized a permanent force in this country to the extent of 5,000 men. I voted for that Bill and I remember it well. We thought that 5,000 men constituted a good, fair standing army, as we called it; but it was never recruited up to that strength. Under Sir Frederick Borden the total force, all ranks, never exceeded 3,050 men; and under my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) I do not think the figures ever reached 3,050. I think they fluctuated between 3,000 and that number. Last year this House of Commons, I think with very little discussion and with very general concurrence, agreed that the permanent force of 'Canada should be increased to 10,000. There was little discussion.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
That is not right.
Mr. CAiSGRAIN:	We voted against it.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

You had the majority to carry it.
Mr. (SPEAKER: Order.

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: At all events, Parliament in its wisdom enacted that there should be an authorized force in this country up to 10,000. No one, I think, had any idea that the force should be recruited up to that number, and the Minister of Militia at the time so stated to the House. But the authority to raise such a force, if it became necessary, was certainly given by Parliament as a precautionary measure. I know that the Government has made public statements that the force would not be recruited beyond 5,000 or half of the total,

speakerposition: subtopic
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
authorized and up to the present moment I can tell my hon. friend from Laprairde that the figures I give him are correct, namely, 3,555 men of all ranks. There is still room to recruit 1,445 more men before we reach the 5,000 limit. I do not know that they will be recruited. In the province of Quebec, particularly in regard to the 22nd Regiment, we are still endeavouring to recruit more men; and I must say that I am a little disappointed to see all over Canada the slowness with which recruiting for the permanent force is being done.
Mr. -CASGRAiIN:	You should not be.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says I
should not be disappointed, but I am. I believe in the maintenance in- this country of a reasonably good militia force. We have always had one since Confederation, and I trust that we shall always continue to maintain one. When I confess that I am a little disappointed at the slowness with which recruits are coming, both in the permanent force and the militia force of Canada, I of course state only my own feelings on the subject. I thought that with the increased rate of pay our permanent units would be filled up, but that is not the case. I find that we still have something to -do in the way of providing for the comfort and convenience of the men, and the greatest drawback at this moment is our lack of barrack accommodation and proper living conditions. During the winter months we suffered from a good many desertions and the reason always given was that, living conditions not being such as civilians would tolerate, there was no good ground for asking soldiers to put up with them. That is one of our difficulties at this moment, and I may refer to it further as I proceed. Now, if we go to the limit contemplated, viz., 5,000, we would require 1,445 more men. Before it became necessary for me to charge my mind with the details of this department, I was a civilian and as such I admit that I misapprehended the real situation, as I know the majority of hon. members misapprehend it. They have not the information, and in the absence of the details they cannot form a proper estimate of the work of the Department of Militia and Defence. ,For the information of the' House I will state what the whole permanent force establishment is. We have the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery stationed at Kingston, a very efficient force, which is used for the training of artillery militia units. That is the main purpose of the permanent force. It is almost, though not 
quite the exclusive purpose. It is our only permanent field artillery. We have only one more regular artillery branch in the service and that is the garrison artillery. These are stationed at Halifax, Quebec and on the Pacific coast. That is all the artillery we maintain in Canada in our permanent force. In regard to infantry, we have the Royal Canadian Regiment, the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry and a new regiment just formed for the purpose of perpetuating in this country the heroic deeds of the men wh8 formed the overseas regiment known as the 22nd, now .a new regiment of the permanent force, established or in process of establishment in the city of Quebec. The three regiments constitute our infantry establishment. In cavalry we have two units, the Royal Canadian Dragoons, and the Lord Strathcona Horse. In addition to the foregoing we hiave the engineering corps, the army service corps, the medical corps, the dental corps, a corps of clerks engaged in the pay office-the army staff clerks I think they are called-and two other corps which we should have but which we have not yet organized, namely, the signalling corps, and the army chaplain corps. All these auxiliary corps are necessary but they entail only a few members. That is our whole establishment. It costs money to maintain it, of course, but its purpose is to look after the whole administration of the militia force in Canada. Now, we have the headquarters at Ottawa land it comes in for a good deal of criticism. It is spoken of as the arm of the service that devotes itself to fuss and feathers. But I can say this much for the headquarters staff-and I did not know it until I was closely connected with that staff-that I have never seen in the Civil Service of Canada or in any business in the country a body of men so loyal to their duty, sot intelligent, so able, and -so hardworking as those who are engaged at the headquarters staff in the city of Ottawa. I have this advantage over all of my predecessors in the office of Minister of Militi.a in that I am surrounded by the ablest and most experienced staff of men who were ever gathered together in Canada. I have on the staff, as the House is aware, as Inspector General, General Sir Arthur Currie, undoubtedly the greatest soldier this country has ever produced and probably one of the greatest soldiers that the world has seen.

making deductions for the changes I mentioned at the opening of my remarks, $12,500,000 represents considerably more than will be actually required for militia expenditure for the fiscal year ending 31s't of March next.
I have not been very long in the Militia Department. I went in there as a civilian. I do not know that it is altogether necessary that the minister who presides over the department should have had ia military training. In Canada I think usually the minister has been a military man to a greater or less degree, but in Great Britain the Secretary of State for war in the majority of oases has been a civilian. However, I am free to admit that when I took charge of the department my knowledge was very hazy and very general, and I do not think I had any real appreciation of the policy or objects of the department; indeed, the knowledge I had then was the common knowledge to be found among civilians throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I have had an opportunity to become familiar with the working and objects of the department. And I have not gone along with my eyes shut. I have noticed some things which I think might be improved, and some of my ideas regarding changes are now under consideration. I recognize also some difficult situations that will have to be faced in the near future, but I think the most pressing need at the present moment is the question of barrack accommodation.
The permanent force is one to be proud of, but we have practically no 'accommodation for it. In Halifax what military barracks we had were badly damaged by the explosion. We have some buildings there yet, I am told, hut while they -may prove suitable and adequate for summer occupation, they are not adapted for housing troops in winter. In Quebec we have barrack accommodation which will not require very much expenditure. In St. John we have only rented accommodation. In Fredericton we have accommodation for a battery. In Montreal we have no accommodation. We have rented property known as the Peel Street Barracks, but we have to give up possession in a couple of months. In Ottawa we have, no barracks; although I think we should have. In Toronto we are perhaps in a worse position than anywhere else. We have the Old Fort, About 120 years old and falling into decay and we have still stationed there the Royal Canadian Dragoons. The property is too small, it is badly situated, it is in bad repair; but, worse than that, it has been disposed of to
the Toronto National Exhibition and our right of occupation ceases on the 1st of July next. In Winnipeg we are fairly well off for accommodation. In Regina we have none, in Calgary we have none, and in Victoria the accommodation is of the slightest kind. That is a very serious problem, because our experience has been that while you may increase the pay of the rank and file in your permanent militia force, unless you give them proper housing conditions and proper surroundings you are not going to retain them.
Well, how is the problem to be met? I find that we have a very large amount of real estate belonging to the Government of Canada but held in right of the Department of Militia and Defence. We have many very valuable properties in Halifax. ;We have in the Rockcliffe Rifle Ranges one of the most valuable properties in this neighbourhood, comprising an area of 500 or 600 acres of the choicest land to be found anywhere, and we do not hold it for any useful purpose. This year the rifle matches will be held on it for the last time. The new 'Connaught Ranges will be used next year for this purpose.

two years ago no loss will be incurred in connection with our selling it as soon as we are able to arrange for its sale. In the meantime, it is being occupied on lease terminable at the end of two years by St. Andrew's College.
There is one other matter to which I should like to direct attention and in connection with which, I think, something might be done. We have in the Department of Militia as fine a corps of engineers as can be found anywhere in the world. We have a great many engineering services in the Government of Canada apart altogether from the Militia Department. I believe that our corps of engineers in the Militia Department could perform all the engineering services of the Government of Canada. All the Government engineering in the United States is performed by the War Office- river, harbour, bridge and construction works, buildings, surveys and the like. Five or six departments of this Government do surveying work; thaj. could all be consolidated into the Militia Department. So with other engineering services. Our graduates from the military college are recognized as among the most capable engineers in the country; the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have no hesitation in taking these men on their staff. I believe that a system could be worked out whereby all the engineering work of the Government could be performed by engineers of the Militia Department and that the result would be a tremendous saving.
One other suggestion-and it is a suggestion of the Inspector General, Sir Arthur Currie. First and foremost among the functions and duties of the Department of Militia is the defence of Canada. The Inspector General is very strong in the view that all branches of that defence should be centred in a single department; that we should have in that department not only our permanent forces and our militia, but also our mounted police, our civil police, our Air Board. The latter is a distinct department to-day, although I have the honour for the time being of presiding over the board as chairman. As time goes on and the work becomes reduced, the work now done by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment might also be brought under the Department of Militia. The Inspector General considers that this matter should have immediate consideration. He thinks that the carrying out of some such plan would result in better co-operation, more efficient co-ordination of work and a tremendous

saving in the carrying on of these various services. These are matters which are now under consideration. As time goes on some of them can certainly be worked out to a conclusion for tlhe general benefit of the country.
As the items of the Estimates are taken up I think I can give pretty full information on the points which will arise. In the meantime, let me say that if you give the question of the proposed militia expenditure the same fair consideration that you would give to it if it were a private matter, a domestic matter, a company matter, a business matter and siay that if six, seven, eight or nine years iago this service would have carried on at $5,000,000, to-day the same service would cost $10,000,000, you will be looking at the matter in a fair way. If hon. members apply that test or that criticism to it I am satisfied that they will agree that the present proposals of the Government are moderate in the extreme.
