giving expression to the 'surprise which must be felit not only in (this House but throughout the country once it is learned that the minister has spent his time not in *seeking to advocate retrenchment in the Department of Militia and Defence, but in endeavouring to excuse increased expenditures at this particular time.
The minister has told us that while the Estimates which have been presented to Parliament for this year show an increase of $4,000,000, the Estimates are, in reality, not made up correctly-that is What his statement amounts to. The Estimates as printed on page 30 indicate that in 1919-20 the several items there set forth totalled $8,369,552, and that this year for the same items, an amount of $12,498,506 is asked. The minister has seen that an increase of $4,000,000 in the expenditures of the Militia Department is one not calculated to meet with approval-throughout the country. Indeed, he has already had evidence of that in the comments on the Militia Estimates that have appeared in the press. So he tells us that the Estimates are not correct; that as a matter of fact moneys appropriated for demobilization purposes were used to meet some of the expenditures that come under the head of Militia and Defence. If that be true it would seem to indicate that the Government had used for one purpose an appropriation which had been made for an entirely different purpose.	.
Mr. GUTHRIEi: If I may he permitted, I made no such statement; I intended to give no such impression. I said that last year certain items were war items and were charged to War Appropriations; this year they are being charged ito Militia and Defence. That is the statement I made, and I think the House understood it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: Well, they are exactly the same class of expenditure. If they .were charged to War Appropriation last year, why are they not charged to War Appropriation this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
We want to terminate
the war if we can, and the war expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
The minister
says ithat he wishes to terminate the war and war expenditure. The minister is re-questiing an appropriation of $38,463,400 for demobilization purposes; I assume that that is the appropriation which would correspond to the War Appropriation of last year. That being so, the minister has in this year's

Estimates another large sum -which must be taken into account along wifth these Estimates which relate more particularly to the Department of Militia and Defence. If the Government follow just the course which they have followed within the past year, we have every reason for assuming that some part of this $38,000,000 now asked for demobilization purposes will be used, as was the War Appropriation of last year, for militia and defence purposes. If the Estimates are wrong, if they have been presented so as to be misleading, the Government must take the blame. The Estimates stand in the form in which they have been presented by the Government to Parliament, and as presented they clearly show an increase of more than $4,000,000 over the amounts that were asked for last year. As I have just said, the minister has made it apparent that last year some of the expenditures came out of the War Appropriation; this year he is asking for a similar appropriation for demobilization purposes. I repeat that unless we can get from the Government a guarantee that no part of that appropriation will be used for militia and defence purposes, we cannot assume that when we come before Parliament next year, there will not again be this difference.
But the point to which I wish particularly to direct attention is the minister's endeavour to draw a comparison between the expenditure on militia and defence at the present time and amounts that were voted prior to the war. The minister seems to think that at the present time we ought to vote an amount at least equal to amounts that were being voted prior to the war. .That is where I take direct issue with him. Before the war it was pretty generally anticipated; it was oertainly said in official quarters that a menace was threatening the world, and that it was necessary to meet that menace by increasing our military and .naval forces. That argument was used as the ground for increasing military expenditures, and it was largely in anticipation of the danger of a great international disturbance that this country voted for military and naval purposes the sums of money which were appropriated at that time. But conditions are wholly different to-day. There is no world menace. Where does the minister expect invasion from? The minister says that this expenditure is needed for the defence of Canada-defence against whom? There is no answer; there is no answer to be made. There is not an hon. gentleman on the other side who will

say that a single nation at the present time has any hostile intention or attitude of hostility towards this country, or that there is the slightest danger of Canada .being invaded from any quarter. Yet the minister asks us to-day to vote a sum that .will bear 'comparison with expenditures .voted on the eve of the terrible situation which occurred in 1914. I might further point out that prior to 1914, that, to be correct, during the period of the Liberal Administration, because the minister referred to that period, we had surpluses, not deceits in our public accounts, and we had a small national debt. To-day we have a colossal public debt; we have obligations that are wholly different, and we are not in the same position to-begin to meet them. It is one thing to lay out sums of money on different appropriations when there are plenty of funds in the treasury, but it is quite another matter when the nation is trying to cope with an enormous deficit and to meet obligations such as the country heretofore has never been faced with, and .when conditions are such that there is the strongest reason why we should economise in every possible particular, and especially in those particulars in which no satisfactory reason can be shown for large expenditures.
But the most important consideration of all is this. The minister has spoken about the need for training camps, permanent barracks and the like. Prior to 1914, it was necessary to have men trained as soldiers; we had no trained men, or very few, .but what is the position to-day? We have in this country to-day an army of trained men, the most efficient soldiers that will .be found in any part of the world, so that the situation is wholly different from what it was prior to the wax. The need fox training to-day is not what is was prior to the war. We have the experience, knowledge, and attainments of thousands of men as our security and safeguard if there be need for such at the present time. That is a reason why, on this particular score, much could be done in the way of reducing expenditures.
The committee, however, should consider, not only what the minister is asking us to appropriate for militia and defence, but what is being spent for military purposes in different directions. First of all, there is the demobilization appropriation of $38,463,400. Under these circumstances, it would not be unreasonable to ask the minister to suspend as largely as possible further outlays for militia and

defence until we have completed voting money for purposes of demobilization. For that period of time until at least we get through with this expenditure of $38,000,000 for demobilization purposes, we are surely justified in objecting to increased expenditures for the purposes of the ordinary work of the Department of Militia and Defence. But we have been vastly increasing expenditures in other directions to meet, in part, the purpose which the minister says will be served by the Department of Militia and Defence. He has mentioned the danger of invasion as one ground for this expenditure, and the other ground is maintenance of peace at home at all times. The other evening we were told by the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) that the mounted police were being increased in order to maintain law and order at home. The Hon. the President olf the Privy Council argued that he believed it was better to decrease the militia and to increase the mounted police, and on that score he sought to have appropriated an item of $4,674,066 for the mounted police. The Government have further placed in the Estimates an appropriation of $500,000 for buildings for the mounted police.-These are items that must be considered in connection with the Militia and Defence Estimates. It da perfectly proper also, in considering defence matters, that we should consider expenditure in connection with naval affairs. This year the Government led us to believe that there was to be retrenchment in that line and that all that would be expended would be $300,000; but in the last couple of days, the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Ballantyne) has told us that when the Supplementary Estimates are brought down, they will contain a further Estimate of $2,200,000 for the purpose of naval defence; and this afternoon we get from the Minister of Militia for the first time, the announcement that he contemplates also in the Supplementary Estimates asking for an additional $2,000,000 for the purpose of building barracks for the permanent force in this country.

speechtext:
If we go on in that wtay, we shall have a military budget of very large proportions. Let me repeat some of the figures:

maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext: We are paying for tht, League of Nations.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: EXCISE TAX RESOLUTIONS CONSIDERED IN COMMITTEE OF WAYS AND MEANS.
speechtext:
-when at this, of all times there is the greatest need for economy and retrenchment, and the least need to fear invasion from any particular source.
These are not the only expenditures that the country is making for military purposes. There are also the obligations arising out of the war. We have an Estimate- and there will doubtless be additional Estimates in this connection also-of $25,825,676 for pensions in connection with the European war and the active militia, $34,000,000 for Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and $50,017,000 for Soldiers' Land Settlement. That is a total of $109,842,676, directly connected with military expenditures that the country has to meet at this time, in addition - to this proposal of some $60,000,000 more for the purposes I have already outlined. I think the country Will be indignant when it discovers that the ministry has forgotten altogether the necessity for retrenchment in this particular line, and I think we on this side of the House will be justified when the Government asks us for the appropriations suggested, in requesting that they be cut down very substantially. I might as well say immediately that we will ask that from some of the items , the Government cut off a very considerable amount of what they are proposing to expend. I mention this now in order that the ministry may consider whether, in view of this summary which I have given of the total expenditure on these particular scores, it is not possible of their own accord to volunteer suggestions as to directions in which retrenchment can be made.
A reference has been made to General Sir Arthur Currie. I have the highest admiration for General Currie, and I am only too happy to have an opportunity of saying, so far as my own individual opinion is concerned, that I agree with every word the minister has said about him. I should like to draw the minister's attention to a remark which I see General Currie made, speaking in this city on Thursday of last

week before the General Assembly. Sir Arthur is reported in the Ottawa Journal of that day, on page 7, as follows:
" We did not intend that militarism should he forced upon this country," General Currie continued, "and just to show you how much of a militarist I am. I may tell you that I told the Canadian Government I would agree to reduce the establishment of the permanent force hy 1,000 men if they would give me instead 1,000 physical instructors who could go through, the country, and impress upon the boys the importance of physical training."
There is a statement- by the expert military adviser to the Government that the permanent force can be cut down by at least 1,000. There is an alternative suggested, which I think is worthy of consideration, but the point I wish to bring out at the moment is that if the permanent force can be reduced by 1,000, there is no need for the Government at this time to ask Parliament for an additional appropriation of over $2,000,000 for barracks for a permanent force.
I think the statement of the minister is amazing when he tells us that the Department of Militia and Defence has property to the value of $3,500,000 or $4,000,000 and does not know what to do with it. Imagine a statement of that kind being made in this Parliament at this time-a statement that we have a department of the Government that has property to the value of $3,500,000 or $4,000,000 that is rendering no service-I think the minister used words to that effect -lands for which there is no particular need at the present time. There is a statement which by itself is deserving of -consideration. I would suggest to the minister that instead of selling this land with a view to raising money to help pay the cost of erecting barracks, he apply the proceeds to run his department, or apply it where it is most needed at the present time to reduce debt instead of incurring further expenditure.
What is it the Government suggests? First that we should hold these lands that we do not know what to do with until we can turn them into a use that will help to perpetuate militarism in some form. Second, that we should sell them to help build barracks for a permanent service so large that we do not already know what to do with, it. This simply shows that as you increase one thing you have to increase all the other elements that go to maintain it. Instead of holding on to these lands for this purpose -seeking to increase the permanent force and building additional barracks to house it- I would suggest that the minister consider retrenchment on all these items and

allow the barracks question to stand over for a time. Let him sell the lands and apply the proceeds to helping the country meet its outstanding obligations at the present time in the manner in which they need so much to be met, and let him give us hope that at least we are getting back to a peace basis, and that the ministry is freeing itself from the war habit of mind into which it has got, and from which it seems so difficult if not impossible for the ministry to free itself.
Hon. Sir,SAM HUGHES (Victoria): Mr. Speaker, I regret I was not present when the minister introduced this subject this afternoon. I was not aware that it was coming up or I should have had the honour of being present and listening to his remarks. I do not know what words the minister uttered regarding General Sir Arthur Currie, and I care not. What I will say is -this: There has ibeen no officer, military or otherwise who has received more commendation by way of propaganda than General Sir Arthur Currie, except maybe the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). I have no objection to anything that may be said about General Sir Arthur Currie, except that the Minister of Militia and Defence or anybody connected with the Militia Department of this country must know that scores of men-I will not say one or two or three, or a dozen -are regarded throughout the length and breadth of this country in military circles as infinitely superior to General Sir Arthur Currie as a general or as -a gentleman.
The question of barracks has been mentioned here -to-day. When I had the honour of being Minister of Militia I started on a policy of erecting drill halls throughout the length and -breadth of this land. I managed to smuggle a large number of them into the Estimates from year to year, and I am satisfied that the people of this country appreciate the value -of these drill halls today. They belong not to- the militaristic, but to the democratic branch of the service. I view with alarm the establishment of police barracks, and of military barracks to any abnormal extent, throughout the length and breadth of this land. I have always claimed that the permanent corps- I am not speaking of the administrative staff-was to a very large extent an excrescence on the country. A country like Canada does not need a large permanent force. In the war, I regret to say, the permanent force did not distinguish themselves at all as compared with the nonpermanent soldiers. It is -a standing joke

in the service that nearly all the soft positions were filled toy permanent corps men. while the boys who went to face the music and bear the brunt of the fighting were the lads belonging to the non-permanent branch of the service. I want to point out in connection with this great dread of insurrection or Bolshevism and all that sort of thing which seems to trouble a great many people in the -Government to-day, that I have Ibeen travelling up and down this country possibly as much as any man in the Government and I have yet to find the first	indication of -any Bolshevik	spiritworthy of notice. I might point out that in 1915, when I had upwards of 375,000 soldiers under arms in -Canada, scattered all over the country, fifteen here, twenty-five there, seventy-five there and a hundred at some	other place,	a -great	manypeople at that time were in dread as to how I was going to control these men. Well	they	are free-born Canadiancitizens, -and being young gentlemen	they	conduct	themselves	with
gentlemanly propriety throughout the land; and after having had the honour of wearing the King's uniform -and defending their country, enduring all sorts of hardships and privations, I see no danger of their misconducting themselves now. I challenge any one to show where a second offence of any serious -character has been brought in the police courts -against any appreciable member of these 375,000 men, and I see no reason why there should now be any need for four or five hundred extra policemen in the country, maintained at an enormous expense. I do not think that we should cultivate a spirit of militarism by building up a great permanent force, but rather that there should be, on the part of the people themselves, free from any military control, the true soldierly spirit of wanting to protect the country in time of need. The military spirit must be in the people as individuals, and if they have a true sense of responsibility they will always be ready to play their part in the defence of their country. Those men who have returned from the war are splendid Canadians, -and they served rtheir country admirably. But there are a number of men who remained at home, such as General Fiset, Etnmett Clarke, and a score of others I could name, who are now taunted every day of their lives by the propaganda from certain quarters-

speechtext: What is the explanation of the increase of $20,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
These are allowances to corps of active militia; they are authorized under articles 445 and 464 of the pay and allowance regulations. They include allowances for command pay and drill instruction; allowance for care of arms; postage allowance, and what are known as contingent allowances. I understand that this is practically the same amount as was voted annually before the war. Last year, as the committee are aware, many of our militia Estimates were in a state of disorganization, due to the recruiting which had gone on during the war. Full allowances were not paid. Certain allowances were made to commanding officers who had managed to keep together the nucleus of a corps. Many of these commanding officers had devoted a great deal of time in connection with their corps to the work of recruiting for the overseas forces and to them limited allowances were made, on a scale, I think, of fifty per cent of the regular allowance. We have provided, of course, for the establishment of a larger number of militia units than heretofore, as I explained this afternoon. The infantry regiments are slightly increased, to the extent of four or five in number,-perhaps six. The number of batteries of artillery is increased by about twenty-five. In addition there will he a machine gun corps. The commanders of these coips will he entitled to the usual pay

and allowances authorized under the pay and allowance regulations. It is to meet these additional charges that the extra $20,000 is asked lor.

The member for West Edmonton (Mr. Griesbaeh) has just taken the opportunity of reading me a little lecture with regard to som# remarks which fell from my lips this afternoon. I do not stand here to retract in the slightest degree what I said to-day, although it was spoken on the impulse of the moment; on the contrary I am prepared, if necessary, to go much further. I pointed out to-day that a propaganda had been carried on to boom Sir Arthur Currie. I am prepared to prove it before a committee of this House. I have documents in my possession which will prove all I have said to-day and much more -that he had been the willing victim, if not the instigator, of one of the most successful propaganda that has been carried on in any land. For instance, on the night of the 29th of September, 1918, newspaper accounts were all drafted and prepared of the capture of Cambrai, the capture of Eamillies and of places in and around the city of Cambrai. Great descriptions were prepared to indicate that Sir Arthur Currie had done this and Sir Arthur Currie had done that-I myself saw a copy of the document. But, Sir, unfortunately instead of the victory which was referred to our poor boys fell that night to the extent of upwards of twenty thousand men and the propaganda had to be held back. But the object of my remarks to-day was not to expose General Sir Arthur Currie, because I created General Sir Arthur Currie. General Sir Arthur Currie was a fairly successful Colonel of a battalion in Victoria at the outbreak of war. One would have naturally supposed that being in command of a battalion he would be one of the first to volunteer. But up to the present hour General Sir Arthur Currie has never volunteered to serve in this war. I found that there was dissatisfaction with the soldier; that everybody seemed to look to Colonel Leekie, to command the brigade from the West.
When I found that out, a friend suggested to me that if I could induce Col. A. W. Currie to come and fight, he might possibly allay the opposition, and as he was not as well known as Col. Leekie, he might be acceptable to some of the battalion. I accordingly wired Col. Currie, as he was at that time, brought him from Victoria to Valcartier, placed'him in command of a brigade, and let me say to my hon.. friend 232
(Mr. Griesbach), who should know the facts of the case, that I retained Col. Currie in command of the brigade under conditions when no other officer in the British Empire would have retained a man under similar conditions. I sent him to the front and I maintained him there. I shall not refer to the fact that for part of two years he allowed another officer, Col. Jack Currie, to remain under the odium of being a coward, of running away and hiding in a British dugout and being kicked out by a British general. I spoke to General Currie about this matter. Indeed, I felt so keenly about the matter that when I met Col. Jack Currie, who was so stigmatized, I declined to shake hands with him, feeling that any officer who was in command as he was should not desert his colours but should stand to his guns. About a year later, in conversation with a British officer, I learned that this man who had gone into the dug-out was a big officer and that he was Col. A. W. Currie. I got the facts sifted out little by little when I was over in the Old Country until the truth was forced upon me that it was not Col. Jack Currie of Toronto who had done the retiring, but Col. Arthur Currie, who commanded the brigade, the Fifth, Tenth, and a couple of other battalions, in the battle of St. Julien.

Did not General Sir
Arthur Currie demand that that statement be taken back, and was it not taken back?

No. General Currie admitted over his own signature that he went into General Snow's dugout. He did not go to Ypres, but he went to Pottinje, which is only 300 yards from the village of Ypres, where General Snow's headquarters were. His statement is that he did not go back to Ypres, but the fact is that he went within 300 yards of it. He admits in his letter that he went there nominally to ask for reinforcements. When we got the facts of the case, we found that General Snow ordered him to leave the dugout and used very strong language, which I shall not mention here.
If such ibe the case, how could General Currie be promoted afterwards as he was?

General Currie was promoted before these facts were known. Had I remained in office six weeks longer, not only General Currie, but several other officers would have been asked to hand in their resignations. I was confusing the two Curries. When General Currie made the definite statement that he had not been



in Ypres, I accepted his *word; but I did not kno-w that he was quibbling on the statement, and that he had gone to the village or farm of Pottinje, which is only 300 yards from the village of Ypres. He admits having gone there and he was ordered out by General Snow. The facts may just as well be known. I was not the man to bring up General Currie's name; but there is an apparent determination on the part of certain gentlemen to force General Currie's name to the front, and by doing so they are backing General Currie in place of better generals than he is or ever knew how to be. Why do they not come out and sing the praises of General Turner and General Lipsett and other generals who have served their country nobly and well and who have no propaganda? But the eternal propaganda seems to be General Currie and General Currie alone. If they want the whole story, we will give them a great deal more than has been isaid. I have not thrown out anything about General Currie; it has been thrown out by this eternal tooting and propaganda in favour of General Currie to the exclusion of Turner, Lipsett and a number of other generals who are infinitely his superior in tactics, strategy and in personal courage. The question of tactics and strategy in this war largely consists in "go on, go on, go on." The plans were laid in the office of General Foch, with the exception of the last Cam-brai fight; I understand that the plans for that battle were the tactics and strategy of General Currie. I have no hesitation in saying that many Canadians would be above the sod to-day if he had not carried out his tactics and strategy in relation to Cam-brai. As is well known and admitted on every hand, the plans for other actions were largely made in -General Fo-ch's office and were so carried out.
I want to correct my hon. friend (Mr. Griesbaoh) in the statement that there is any personal animus on my part towards General Currie. I created him; I backed him as no person ever before backed another in the history of warfare; I saw him through again and again; but when I found out over this Jack Currie matter that General Currie was the man that was there and that he was quibbling over the statement that he was not at Ypres, I had no great respect for General Currie's honour as a man in relation to his duty towards his fellowman as exemplified in his conduct towards Col. Jack Currie. As regards my carrying on of a propaganda against General Currie, wha{ I have dope is- to [Sir Sam Hughes.)
stand by the rights of other officers. I consider General Turner-and I think I am as competent a judge as is in the Dominion or in the Empire; if I do say that myself, I have proved it-
Oh, oh.

A smirk and a smile are easy, but I want to tell the -Minister of -Militia and other hon. members who smile, that my record is there and shows that if my plans had been carried out from beginning to end, there would have been a different showing in this war. I will stand by the gentlemen whom I know to be true and gallant soldiers, who deserve something done for them by the Government of this country in place of having to read every day of their lives about propaganda in favour oif General Currie, who is unfit-and I say so advisedly-to be compared with them as a general and who is not their equal in other regards.

When we take these proposed increases into account, along |witlh the intention which wae expressed by the *miimieter this alftetmoon of asking Parliament in the course of the next few days for an additional $2,000,000 to establish barracks at different points throughout this country for a permanent force, and take into account also the proposal of the President of the Privy Council JMr. Rowell) for an additional $500,000 for the mounted police, it is perfectly evident that the Government has made up its mind to substitute for a militia in this country <a standing army, and' that we lane (facing ia/t the moment (the niuoleius of a, standing army in Canada. ously as it possibly can be by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. We do not wish to impair in any way the efficiency of ithe militia service of this country. Notwithstanding the information that I sought to give to my hon. friend this afternoon he still seeks to make comparisons between this year's proposal and last year's proposal, and because this item exceeds by $20,000 the item of last year, he says it should be reduced by that amount. How many units are
actually reorganized and active, instead of being simply on paper as mentioned by the minister a few moments ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The city corps are fairly well organized. There are 68 of them and their strength is estimated at 30,000. The rural divisions are not scrwell organized. I doubt very much whether in the province of Ontario there are -more than t-wo or three fully organized rural battalions. Some of them are organized ten, some twenty, some twenty-five, and some thirty per cent of their strength. The artillery batteries are organized -to the extent- of about 50 per cent. The machine gun units are all organized and the officers have been appointed, but they are only recruited up to about 20 per cent of their strength up to the present time. The cavalry regiments are all organ-

ized and officers appointed, the regiments being recruited up to abou/fc 15 per cent of their strength.
