speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have not that information here or I would be very glad to give it. My hon. friend will find it in the red book called the Militia List.
Who appoints the officers commanding these new corps?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The officer commanding is selected by a Selection Board. In the first place, the old officers of the regiment are called together and express their choice by a vote. The name submitted goes before a board specially charged with the selection of officers. After the 'board passes upon the name, it is submitted to the Inspector-General, and if approved by him goes before the Militia Council. If approved, it then goes to the Privy Council, and when approved there, the appointment is gazetted.

What about the other
officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The commanding officer selects his own officers and submits the list to the officer commanding the district to which the regiment belongs. When approved there, the list is forwarded to headquarters.
Would the minister give the names submitted to the Militia Council for the Quebec regiments?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean all Quebec regiments?
No, the Quebec City regiments.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
want the names of the men selected?
I understood by what the minister said that the old officers of each battalion would meet and vote and then the names would be forwarded to the Militia Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The names would be forwarded in the first instance to the district commanding officer.

Has the minister the
names?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not, but I think I could get them from the deputy. The officer of the 9th Regiment is Colonel Chau-

veau; we cannot give the name of the officer for the 8th Regiment at the present time. These are both Quebec regiments. I believe they are the only city corps in Quebec.
What is the war record of Colonel Chauveau?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understand his services were exclusively within Canada. I do not know the circumstances, but I must inform the committee in these matters I do not interfere in any way with the selections made by my responsible advisers. In every case I accept their recommendations, and of necessity I would not know the individual qualifications of the men. I could have the record of this officer looked up and furnish it to my hon. friend at a later date if he desires.

Colonel Chauveau was one of those excellent officers who served in Canada. He is a gentleman with a large family and when the war broke out he commanded the Rimouski regiment in Canada, securing volunteers.
Mr. LAPOINTE Colonel Piuze was in charge of the Rimouski regiment.

Colonel Piuze commanded it when it went to the front, but Colonel Chauveau had charge of the regiment in this country and turned out a fine body of men for Colonel Piuze to take overseas. Colonel Piuze would be one of the first men to say that Colonel Chauveau gave him every assistance.
There is no doubt about that.

I was instrumental in keeping Colonel Chauveau at home for organizing purposes' of a very useful character. He could not very well be spared to go to the front at that time, and as Colonel Piuze was a younger man we kept Colonel Chauveau for organizing purposes. He is one of the best organizing and military officers in Canada.

In the city of Quebec Colonel Chauveau is known as one of the best militia officers. As commanding officer of the 9th Battalion he will do well, and if the Government always chose as wisely as they did in this instance there would be fewer complaints.

I should like to make a few observations which will differ

from the views expressed by my hon. friend from Skeena (Mr. Peek). I desire to make these observations at this moment in order to shorten, so far as I am concerned, the proceedings in regard to the rest of the militia votes. My hon. friend said that there was an impression in a good many quarters that the militia had been starved in Canada. Well, I feel that I am on sure ground when I tel'l him that, on the other hand, there is a very widespread feeling from one end of Canada to the other that it is very doubtEul indeed whether the people have got the full value for what they have spent. That is the other side of the question, and I am not going to argue it; it exists in the public mind. My hon. friend, in a sentence preceding that in which he spoke of the starved militia, told us that the artillery branch-I think that is what he said-was the most efficient in the Canadian army.
I rise to a point of order. I say that the hon. member is exceeding the limits of the item under discussion.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I point out-
I ask for a ruling.
Surely the question of starving or feeding high the militia of Canada [DOT]comes under a proposal to reduce the vote.

I ask for a decision on my point of order, Mr. Chairman. I understand that when this item was first discussed the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) made a speech along general fines. He was followed by' the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbaeh), who also spoke on general lines.
I thought it was on General Currie.

The Chairman afterwards ruled that we would not be allowed to go beyond the strict limits of the item under consideration, and I contend, Sir, that a general discussion of the militia is now out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must point out to
the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) that no general discussion has taken place, especially in .so far as the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Griesbaeh) is concerned, because he has not spoken since the House resolved itself into Committee of Supply.
He spoke to-night while I was here.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was in the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: While the hon. member for Dorchester is quite right in saying that a general discussion of militia Estimates, or a discussion of all the affairs concerning the militia of Canada, would not be in order, I am not prepared to say that the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer have gone to that extent. I do not yet feel obliged to call him to order.

If I may interpose at this
time, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Red Deer has the floor.

I was trying to- give
reasons, arising out of the views of our people on general military expenditure, why I shall vote for the reduction of $20,000 in this particular item. It appears to me that general observations on that question have a distinct hearing on the vote. I was saying that my hon. friend when he spoke of the starved militia, had preceded that remark by the statement that the artillery branch was the most efficient arm of the Canadian army. Now, if a starved militia in peace time makes the most efficient service in war time, my hon. friend's argument is rather in favour of a reduction. And there is this further general consideration, which also has a bearing on the, point, namely, the the Canadian army, the product of two or there short years in a country small, as to population and probably the most peaceful that entered the war, nevertheless was such as to carry as .much terror to the hearts of the enemy as any other branch of the Allies.
Order.

My hon. friend further argued foT a strong voluntary service. On that point he did not quite argue on the same lines as the minister. The minister is of .course anxious to get his vote, and he recommended it to the committee, not along the lines of providing a strong voluntary service, but because, although there are 25 new units, they are not recruited up to full strength. While hi.s military follower recommended this vote on the ground of .a strong military force, my hon. friend the minister took exactly the opposite ground. On that point a very practical consideration arises in my mind. My hon. friend says that there are twenty-five new units and that these are necessary to get all classes of military service .represented icn the militia of Can-

ada. He says they are not recruited up to full strength. But, let me tell my hon. friend and the committee, that is just how militarism grows in a nation. We are told to-night that this vote should be given because these units are not up to full strength. I put it to you and to the committee: Will it not be the endeavour of those who are specially interested in militarism to get the units recruited to full strength at the earliest possible moment? That has been the history of militarism in all the nations of Europe. It will be its history here and it iis for that reason that I at any rate want to guard myself by voting correctly on this item and on the general principle that our people are opposed to militarism. If the leasons of the late war are properly learned they have surely proved that the way to win a war is to have a good cause, a strong people and, above all things, the last shot in the locker.
That brings me to what is, after all, the most important consideration to guide the committee at this time in their general attitude towards military expenditures. My hon. friend talks of making the expenditure equal to that before the war. I am not sure whether the leader of the Opposition did not approve of that attitude in a moderate or mild way.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Not at all.

The state of the finances of this country should be paramount in our minds on this and all branches of expenditure, and that is a point, which has been raised by others, that I desire to press home with all the strength of conviction and of expression I am capable of. We had a prosperous country before the war. We had a government in prosperous conditions financially. Thank God, we have a prosperous country yet which, if wisely governed, will bear all the burden that the war has cast upon it. But a wise government must be forthcoming, and it is not wise to multiply certain lines of expenditure to the enormous sum of $60,000,000 at a time when we are having to impose taxes of a totally new description, whose outcome is so doubtful, to meet this and other expenditures. We must get new taxation-yes, Sir, but we must cut down expenditures, and if we do not cut them on Estimates like this I do not know where we are going to begin.

I really feel that I should say that if a former remark of mine may have offended the hon. member for Dor-

Chester (Mr. Gannon) I certainly spoke with a great deal of haste. I feel very strongly on the question of the Militia Estimates and of the militia of this country. If I did offend the hon. gentleman it was not meant from my heart. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mir. Glark),. whom I agree with on economic questions probably more than any one in this House, made some broad statements against the Militia Estimates. I am going to ask my hon. friend: Are we going to defend this country or not? How are you goinig to defend it, if you have not a strong militia system? My hon. friend made some comparisons in regard to the militia before the war. It is our pride to think of what this country did in the war. Here we were, a young, untried nation. Nobody knew what we could do. They looked upon us as sort of Eskimos, or Indians that were buried in the snow. But, this young nation entered the war. The supreme moment came. Our soldiers went forth on the great battlefields of France and Flanders, where nations had struggled for centuries for the mastery of the world, and achieved great victories against the best army the world had ever known. But at the same time I do not know that they would have achieved any great victories if they had had no training. We wish to train our militia under the voluntary system and to bring them to a state of perfection.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I think the hon. member is going far beyond the limit. He is discussing and paying a tribute to what has been done during the war. I agree with him upon that point,, but on other-occasions the Chair has held that it would not be proper to discuss ^those matters on these Estimates.
There is one single word I wish to say-
Mr. Chairman,. I want a decision on the point of order.
Does the hon. gentleman (M,r. Tweedie) wish to speak to the point of order?
No, Air. Chairman.

I do not want to stir up any more discussion of this nature, but I think we should all act as good, loyal Canadians in support of the minister on these Alildtia Estimates. Therefore, I am not going to interpose such remarks as I have been

making if they are going to offend hon. gentlemen opposite.
They do not offend me at 'all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The point of order
raised by the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caegrain) is that the remarks of the hon. member for Gkeena (Mr. Peck) are not relevant to the item under consideration. I am not prepared to draw the line quite so severely as the hon. member for Charlevoix would have me draw it. I consider that the existence of the active militia of Canada and what it accomplished during the late war have a great deal to do with the vote of an allowance to the officers of the active militia, and in view of the fact that my hon. friend from Charlevoix voted just a moment .ago that more latitude should be given, I would not feel justified in calling the hon. member for Skeena to order.

I wish to say one or two words with regard to the appropriation, whether that appropriation may relate to the naval, police or military service which we have under consideration at the present moment. The first, fundamental principle of any government is that we maintain peace and order throughout the length and breadth of our country from the Atlantic to the Pacific from the North to the South. I was very much surprised to read in the newspapers the utterances of one of the officers of one of the most prominent associations in this country, Mr. C. G. MacNeil, chief secretary of the Great War Veteran's Association. I trust that the newspaper report of his remarks is incorrect, and, if so, everything I say in regard to this question I shall very gladly withdraw. But, if that report is correct, we have a body of men in this Dominion who say that if they cannot .accomplish what they desire by peaceful means, they will do so by a revolution. That is what a representative of the 500,000 or 600,000 .men who fought in the great war is reported to have said: If you do not give us what we ask, then we shall have a revolution corresponding to the Russian revolution. Every one realizes-
Order, order.
There is no order.
Order, order.
Every one is aware that so far as the revolution in Russia is concerned-
Order, order.

-that so far as that revolution is concerned, even the American Federation of Labour which met in Montreal to-day, said: We will not back up that revolution, because its leaders do not represent the majority of the Russian people. When any man-
Order, order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Under the ruling given a few moments ago, the horn, member in discussing the revolution in Russia is somewhat far afield from the item before the committee. I presume that he is referring to that revolution by way of comparison, but a strict interpretation of the rules would oblige me to declare that such a reference is not in order.	.
M,r. TWEEDIE: Mr. Chairman, I always bow to your rulings, because I regard them as the rulings of a gentleman who is eminently qualified toi fill the position he occupies, and I shall refrain from any further reference to the revolution in Russia. But I want to tell this House that when ianv man-I care not whether he is a Tory or a Grit-
Or a Unionist?

-or a Unionist, or a Labourite, or a U.F.O., or a Great War Veteran's representative, or any one else- when lie states that if a mandate issued on behalf o.f any organization is not complied with revolutionary means will be adopted to force compliance, then I say: Let us vote not only wh*t the Minister of Militia asks for in this case, but let us vote more if it is absolutely necessary to maintain the honour, the dignity and the order which must be maintained in this country.
Some hem. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
We are fighting for a few paltry dollars, but when we get utterances from men, who supposedly occupy prominent positions, that they will resort to revolution to enforce their claims-
Order.

-I say-
Some bon. MEMBERS: Order, order.
Go on.

My hon. friends isay ''Order, order." If they will take up the newspapers of Tuesday morning they will find a report of the meeting in this city that I refer to. I want to point out to

them that I premised my remarks by stating that they were based on the supposition that the report is correct. It the sneaker at that meeting contradicts that report and says that he is not in favour of revolution, then my remarks fall to the ground. But if there is any man in the Dominion, I care not who he is-

Louder. *
Mr. TW'EEDIE: -if he talks about revolution, I say: Let us vote this Estimate, and let us vote as much more money as imay be necessary in order that we may maintain order-
'Some hon. MEMBERS: Order.
-and maintain the authority of our Government, I do not care which party is in power.

Mr. Chairman, I fail
to see how my hon. friend (Mr. Tweedie) will remedy the condition he is lamenting by increasing the vote for the militia. If there is one branch of governmental activity as to which the people of this country are opposed at the present time to grant any increased expenditure it is the Militia Department. It is all very well to say that in the pre-war period we were spending as much money as is asked for by this present item, but, as has been pointed out, there was money to spend at that time. Conditions have changed, and to-day we are facing an enormous debt,-a debt which cannot be paid by us but which future generations will have to discharge. At this time, when the people are bled white by taxation; this Government is juggling with taxes,-the taxes change colour every day, and we do not know to-day what new taxes will be imposed to-morrow. And why this heavy taxation? Because this enormours debt has been incurred to pay the expenses of a war that was to end all wars. That was the argument used in all parts of this country. This Parliament was elected and this Government was formed, it was alleged, to bring the war to a successful conclusion and so end all wars in the future. Yet we are asked to-day to vote an increased amount for the militia. I say that the people everywhere are opposed to any such increase. I can fairly judge public opinion as it is expressed in the newspapers of the country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and I find that every one 'is in favour of reducing our military expenditure. Why should we increase it? At the present time a League of Nations has been formed, we
[Mi-. Tweedie.]
are sending a representative to all its conferences, and we are paying our share of the money necessary to support that League. Other countries are decreasing their military expenditures, in spite of what has been said on the other side. I was reading an article in a newspaper to-day stating that in Great Britain a League to End War has been formed. Many men prominent in politics, in church and in civil life are members of that League, as also are gentlemen who served in the war cabinet of Britain. A deputation from that League had an interview with the cabinet of Mr. Lloyd George and asked for a reduction in military expenditures, and asked also that steps be taken for the purpose of avoiding future wars. They stated that the best means to accomplish this was to reduce military expenditures and to stop the manufacture of munitions and other war materials. The old saying that "if you want peace you must prepare for war," has been proved a fallacy, and people no longer believe it. It is sedulously circulated by the manufacturers of munitions.
Now, my hon. friends on the other side ask: Why did you oppose this special item? We are opposed to the whole increased expenditure on the militia. This item will have the fate of the other items, and II for one am going to vote for the amendment. My last word to the minister is: Accept the suggestion that our expenditure be not increased in any manner whatever. If we have any money to spend, let us spend it to cultivate the arts of peace.
What has taken place with regard to military and naval appropriations in Japan?

If my hon. friend is going to take Japan as his model, I am not going to take Japan as mine. I am a Canadian, and as some hon. members have said, let us give an example to Japan, not take one from her.

I do not want to take Japan as a model, but my hon. friend knows well that the recent war appropriations of Japan have been heavier than they were at any time during the war; they are proportionately heavier than those of any other country in the civilized world. My hon. friend's altruistic ideas may be very good. It is true that Great Britain and her colonies were in a state of unpreparedness when the great war broke out. I tell you that you must be prepared to meet your enemy.
Who is the enemy?
We must have a naval policy in the Dominion of Canada and a small -start involving an expenditure of $2,500,000 is the very best start that we can make.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Tweedie) ought to be reminded, I think, that Japan was an ally of Britain throughout the war and that Canada's coasts on the West were protected by Japanese fleets during the war.
Do you suppose that the Dominion of Canada-
Mr. Chairman-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has the floor.
I would like to know whether I have to give way to all the lawyers in the House. If I have, then I will do it.
Let the Doctor speak.

Not being a lawyer, I
find it somewhat difficult to follow the reasoning of some hon. members who have presented itheir views. My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) condemns this item because there is an increase of $20,000 over the similar item of last year. He says that this is all wrong; that we should cut down our militia; that we were justified in time of peace in voting a similar amount for this purpose because, he says, we had the money then ito spend. His argument, in effect, is that there was no need for the militia then, 'but that we had the money and that we were justified in throwing it to the four winds. The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) takes a somewhat similar view. He asks:	"Why this expenditure? What
enemy are you preparing to meet?" Well, if the hon. member takes that line of argument, what need is there for this expenditure at all? If he dismisses the question with the statement that there is no need for this vote because there is no prospective enemy against whom we have to guard, and if that argument holds good in regard to an increase of $20,000 in the item now under consideration, it holds goods with regard to every dollar voted for Militia and Defence. In the past we have voted millions of dollars in times of peace for militia purposes. There is no doubt that although the war is over there have been evidences of unrest in various pants of the 233
country, as there have been in practically every country of the world. I am not in favour of throwing money about broadcast in militia matters. I do not believe in militarism, but I do believe in sustaining a force sufficient to maintain the dignity of Canada and to maintain order in (this country in case of necessity. The minister has not exceeded the bounds of reason in asking the committee to give him a vote for $1-20,000 to meet the necessary expenses of those who will be called upon to form the personnel of Ithese various units. Having regard to increased costs, $20,000 strikes me as an exceedingly moderate increase in -connection with this item. The minister is keeping his militia Estimates well with in the bounds of what we considered right and proper before there was any war; in other words, he is keeping them within reasonable limits.

My criticism was based
on the statement of the minister that he is increasing the artillery units and other arms of the service over and above what we had in pre-war days. I think that the committee is entitled to know why he is doing that. The minister states that there will be an increase of twenty-five artillery units but no increase in the personnel. Well, an increase in the number of units will inevitably lead to an increase in the personnel, and that it the point upon which I based my criticism. My hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) leaves it to be inferred that an increase in the military establishment is necessary to keep order in Canada. The other night when the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), brought up his Estimates for the mounted police, he said that it was necessary to maintain a force of this kind for the preservation of law and order. I quite agree that if anything of this kind becomes necessary it is better to use a police force than to call out the militia. But I do not think it is necessary to have these forces to maintain law and order in Canada. The people of Canada are a law-abiding people. The surest way to invite disturbance is to leave the impression upon ithe minds of the people thalt they are liable to be put down by armed forces.

May I ask my hon.
friend a question?
No.

I was directing my question to the hon. member for Marquette



(Mr. Crerar), not to any one else. The member for Marquette, if he admits the necessity for having, we will say, fifty militia units, will admit that with the expansion of ithe country and the opening up of new districts you cannot keep the number of units down to where it was ten or twelve years ago. If you make provision at all for militia and defence you must make provision for the expansion of the country and the opening up of new districts.

My hon. friend made an argument rather than asked a question, but I am prepared to answer his question. I do not think there is any necessity or justification for increasing the number of artillery units when we consider the amount of taxes the people of this country will have to contribute for federal purposes. That simply emphasizes the fact that there is no justification for the increase.

I desire to say a
word or two on behalf of the Estimate as presented by the minister. I regret very *much that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has considered it desirable and wise to question an increased expenditure of $20,000 over last year. There is no doubt, as has been very frequently shown in this House, that Canada is the most poorly defended country in the world to-day, and when the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), recommend that we begin disarmament, we have not in this country anythinng to begin to disarm as armaments go. The minister has told us that the United States are voting $480,000,000 for their army, and according to their' own statement, they are going to have the largest navy in the world in 1924. Therefore, my hon. friends, who rely upon the defence of the League of Nations, who put their faith in the League of Nations-
Order.

My hon. friend (Mr. Lapointe) stated that he put his faith in the League of Nations, and that was not disputed by my hon. friends opposite as being the correct argument. I do not want to discuss the League of Nations; I only mention it. I say: Do not put your trust in .the League of Nations, but put it in the Estimates of the Minister of Militia, which are of a very modest character. I come from a city that has a few militia units in

it. I know something of the self-sacrifice of the officers and men in those units, and they spend a great deal of their own money and an immense amount of their time in their country's service. That is what the militia of Canada has done for many years. ,The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) says that the end of all wars is at hand, but I do not agree with him. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) says that we have just fought a war to end war, and that that was said on the platform in our part of the country. I was on a good many platforms, and I told every audience that I addressed on this question that they need not look for the *end of all wars in our time or within a thousand years, unless humanity was entirely reconstructed from his boots to the top of his head. As long as humanity is as it is, we are going to have wars; and whether you have a league of nations or anything else, you must have a force that you can call to your aid when diplomatic effort fails. The hon. member for Marquette asked us to name the enemy that this appropriation is going to help to defend us against. It is not necessary to name an enemy; it would be a very unwise proposition to name an enemy, and my hon. friend, as a former minister of the Crown, ought to know that if we thought there was an enemy, the last thing we should do would be to name him. Let me instance to my hon. friend what might occur, and what I think he will agree might occur. There is a possibility that the United States and Japan might go to war.
Order.
I say that is a possibility, and if such a thing-
Mr. Chairman-
If such a thing happens-

I rise to a point of order. I think the hon. gentleman has no right to discuss the international relations of different countries, and in support of my contention I might quote to the Chairman a decision recently given by a Speaker of the British House of Commons-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before calling the
hon. member to order, I wished to' see to what extent the remarks which he was proceeding to make referred to the item under discussion. If they are used as an argument to justify his vote in favour of this item in the Militia Estimates or if they are

used as an argument against the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition, they would be in order. Until I have ascertained if they are to be so used I cannot call the hon. member to order.
Now that the cannons of Dorchester have ceased to thunder for a moment, I will proceed.
Give us a plough.

I was going to state that in order to keep out of the war, a force would .be necessary in Canada. Anybody knows that to break neutrality draws you into .the war, and with a militia and a standing army as weak as we have we would have only live or ten men per mile of our frontier to see that neutrality was observed and to keep ourselves out of the war. It is necessary in order that we might even observe neutrality and keep ourselves out of the war to see that no act of war is permitted on our side of the line from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That is not an easy matter, because the whole frontier would have to 'be policed. Therefore, the Minister of Militia is asking for a very modest amount to overtake what .might ibe considered a very grave -situation in case anything of that kind occurred. As to all wars being ended, my hon. friends- might as well say that all fires are ended because we have had an enormous conflagration that has burned up everything within a certain area and, therefore, we should discontinue insurance because no more fires are going to take place. As long as there is property left to bum, you are going to have fires; and as long as you have danger of fire, you want insurance, and this is a simple mattSr of insurance for the benefit of Canada, for the benefit of its citizens. Therefore it is only wise and, I think, a very moderate position that the minister takes when he asks us to vote only a few hundred thousand dollars. If the amount were $10,000,000 or $25,000,000, I would hold up both hands for it, and I am a man of peace; I have always been a man of peace.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends opposite are very fond of a scrap with the tongue in political matters; but if they think it is not at all possible that we should ever come to blows, I hope we shall not; but I submit that the incendiary .speeches our hon. friends sometimes make lead to wordy conflicts, and wordy conflicts sometimes lead to blows between nations, and we have going on in the -world to-day a large quan-233J
tity of that. Therefore, it is only wise and considerate of this country and its citizens that -we should have a militia force and, I should say, a small army as well-and it is a very small army, 7,000 men, I believe, all told. We cannot maintain our dignity and self respect in a League of Nations or amongst the nations of the world unless we have something to show that, if war breaks out amongst humanity, we are going to bear our share of the white man's burden .according to our population and the extent of territory we have to defend. I trust my hon. friend across the way will withdraw his amendment and let -this appropriation go through, because the .amount is very moderate.
Amendment negatived: yeas 54, nays 69.
Before the vote is registered I would like to ask if the vote given by the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) has been counted?
Does the hon. member want to know what I was voting on?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Assistant Clerk informs me that the vote of the hon. member for West Hamilton was not counted. I might point, out that according to Parliamentary authorities the rule governing the vote in Committee of the Whole, is that any hon. member who is present in the Chamber when the vote is counted, has the right to vote. This is absolutely contrary to the rule governing the votes taken in special committees of the House and to that governing the vote in the House. I have never found a justification for the custom, but it is in existence, and therefore if the vote of the hon. member for West Hamilton had been counted, it would have been quite legal.
I would ask the hon. member for West Hamilton to tell us what he was voting on? Would the minister tell us how many cavalry officers have been appointed under this organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have not the information here but I could give it to the hon. member the next time the Estimates are up.
What is the mode of appointing these cavalry officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend must have been out of the House, because this is the third time I have given this information. The recommendation for a commanding officer goes first to a board of selection from

the old officers of the regiment. After being passed upon by that board, the name is submitted- to the Inspector General. If approved by him, it is submitted to the Militia Council, and if approved by that Council, it goes to the Privy Council -when, if approved, the appointment is gazetted. Every commanding officers is entitled to make his own slate of officers for his unit. He submits his slate to the commanding officers of the military district, who, if he approves, forwards it to headquarters, where it is dealt with, and the names are gazetted as in the case of the appointment of commanding officers. If the commanding officer of the district disapproves, the list is not forwarded, as a rule.
What is the increase in the number of cavalry officers appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There have been twelve cavalry regiments organized to date, and there would be about twenty-four officers to each regiment.
About how many of an increase in the number of cavalry officers appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My information is that there is no increase.
The minister told us that there was a decrease in the number of men from 100,000 to 80,000. Has there been a corresponding decrease in the number of officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The units have not been recruited. Many of them are recruited up to only 10 per cent of their strength, and the organization in some cases is only on paper, but they are starting out this week to get their men. Other units are recruited up to forty or fifty per cent; I should say that from fifty to sixty per cent is the highest. The proposal is based upon the number of regiments which I gave to the House. If these do not- materialize the money will certainly not be spent, -but we have to estimate for sufficient money to cover the possible expenditure. '

What
will happen if a rural regiment, for example, is recruited only up to ten per cent of its strength? Will the regiment be kept alive? Or will it be disbanded? What percentage is necessary in order to make it advisable to go on and train the regiment?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If a regiment should be recruited only up to ten per cent pf its strength it would be disbanded. I am hopeful that we shall do better than that. If 
fifty per cent of the strength is not obtained the regiment is disbanded.
What percentage of officers, and what percentage of men is required if the regiment is to continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have provided in the Estimates for training eighty per cent of the full establishment. We shall not get that percentage, but that is the basis of the estimate.

I would like to
point out the importance of this item providing for allowances to officers of the active militia. The history of the war shows that a. country without a militia is not nearly up to the level in manhood of a country with a trained militia. I suggest with all kindness that it would be the very best thing for the country if in every riding in Canada we had a militia corps in which all the young men could enroll. It has been pointed out again and again, as the records show,

and the clergymen of the country are behind the movement, realizing the strength of it,-that morally, mentally, physically and spiritually, the man who serves and has training in the militia of the country is better than the man who lacks that training. It has a tendency to build up a manly pirit, and among the lads who have returned from the front you will scarcely find one who has not improved physically, unless he has suffered wounds or been incapacitated. Those men who have not been injured are physically better as a result of their exertions, and their service has meant character and energy and inspiration to them. They are better than before they went into the service. And I would suggest to my hon. friends on both sides who have not joined the militia that they should do so and take the training afforded. At the end of six weeks or two months, I venture to say, there is not one of them who would not endorse every item the Minister of Militia presents to them along the line of a non-permanent active militia.
Annual Drill, $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This item for annual drill brings very forcibly. before us the situation in regard to expenditures and the possibilities of economy. In the general discussion we have gone over a good deal of ground, and mention has been made of the enormous expenditures with which the country is faced. I should like to remind thfe committee alt this stage, of the debate which we have just had on the

Budget and the figures which have been placed before Parliament by the Minister of Finance. I will not quote more than the Finance Minister's 'statement, in his introductory remarks, that at the present time the gross debt of Canada, according to the ledger, is $3,014,483,774.12 and the net debt $1,935,946,312.85.

I rise to a point of order.
I believe there is a rule of the House that provides that an hon. member speaking to a motion in any debate cannot refer to matters that have been brought out in any previous debate of the same session.

You will not expedite
business by these little exceptions, Brother Morphy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I cannot understand why my hon. friend has risen to a point of order. When we are discussing Estimates and the amounts to be expended in 'this country, if we are mot to be permitted to mention what the national debt is, then whalfc a,re we to be allbwed to talk about? We are confronted with the glaring fact that this nation at- this moment has a gross national debt of $3,014,483,774.12, with a net debt of $1,935,940,312.85 which, as the Minister of Finance pointed out, is increased, after certain accounts are taken into consideration, to $2,273,305,436.92. We have been told by the Minister of Finance that the only possible way in which this debt can be reduced is by increased production on the one hand and retrenchment in expenditures on the other. Now, Sir, this item asking for $1,500,000 for annual drill compels ns to -a.sk whether -at this particular time we -are justified, in view of the ple-a of the Minister of Finance for increased production in order t-o m-eet the public debt -and! the ordinary expenditures of the country, in having any -annual drill at all this year which will take from the farms -and factories men who are needed first -and foremost for productive purposes. I would point out that we have in this country at the present time -an army of experienced men who need no drilling, -men who have been through the war and have suffered its hardships. No amount of drilling in the world will make them more efficient -than they are to-day, and until we are -through with the work of demobilization we can well afford to dispense altogether with annual drills. That is the -position which we on this side of the Ho-use take on this question, and we take that position on two grounds: First, that for the purposes
of increased production, which is_ most essential at the present time, we should encourage men to engage actively in every work that will tend to that end. not even withdrawing them temporarily at this particular season; second, that if we can save a million and a half or a million and a quarter dollars on something that is wholly unnecessary, it is a saving which is all to the good at this time. Let me ask the committee a question. Last year the annual drill wras dispensed with: Is there a single member of the House, or a single man or woman in the country, who feels that we are- -any -t.he less secure in Canada to-day th-an if we had had that drill? And I ask the same question so far as the annual drill this year is concerned. If that drill is to be held it must be held within the next two months. Is there any hon. member in -this House, or any m-an in the country who believes that the people will be one whit securer after the annual drill thi-s year th-an they are at this moment? The item is wholly unnecessary and unwarranted under the circumstances that exist to-day. . We have in ou;r hospitals at the present time hundreds of men returned from overseas who are -still requiring treatment; and there are so-ldie-rs to-day wh-o are asking for something more in- the way of increased pensions. Is it going to -allay feeling through-out the country to have these -annual parades at this particular season? I think the people of this nation have witnessed enough to recall the frightfulness of war, and -a -rest from that sort of thing for at least a period of on-e year wi-lli do much good while it can- do n-o possible harm.
Somethi-ng has been said to-night about increasing these expenditures rather than reducing them. Well, to what will that increas-ed expenditure lead if not to bankruptcy? And of what use will it be to a bankrupt nation to have men for military or naval, purposes, no- matter tow numerous they be? We must get- on a sound financial footing as quickly as possible. When we reach the -position, in -which our ifin-an/ces are sound, then we can afford these extra expenditures if the demand for them should exist. But it has n-ot been shown so far that there exists o.n the pa-rt o-f any individual any fe-a-r from invasion, or that there is any need of an annual drill <fosr the purpose of maintaining law and-order at ho-m-e. I move, therefore, that this item be reduced by $1,150,000, which is the increase over and -above the amount that was voted by the committee last year. In
3676 '

my opinion the whole item should be struck out. But, inasmuch as last year $350,000 was voted I see no objection to our allowing the Government that amount as there may be something we are not aware of at the moment which would require a small expenditure in connection with this particular item. At any rate an increase over and above what was allowed by this Parliament last year for annual drill is wholly unwarranted. No grounds have been given Why this increase should be made. Therefore I hope the committee will support this resolution to save the country at this time this $1,150,000.
Let me just add this further point: We have been imposing new taxes on the consumers of this country and every man, woman and child who is obliged to pay any part of the increased taxes which have been imposed as a result of the discussions that we have had in the last day or two, will contribute in some measure to these military expenditures. If we allow these expenditures which are unnecessary at the present time to. be kept up to the figure asked by the minister we will have to wait just so -much longer before these excess, or excise, taxes, as they are called, can be withdrawn from the people of Canada. Now is the time to economize, now is the time to produce; this is not the time to withdraw men from production ot to increase expenditures which can Teturn no value to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As near as we can estimate it will require $953,548; that is the total under this item that we expect to spend.
What was the amount expended before the war for the drilling of city regiments?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot give the figures to-night, but they could be ascertained and I could let my hon. friend have them at a later period of the discussion.-
Mr. LAPOINTE': I think we should have that information before voting this amount. We are told that this item is only for the purpose of the annual drilling of city regiments. Surely we are entitled to know what was the cost of that drilling before the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend as wrong in confining the amount to city regiments. This includes alsoi the permanent force which is drilled every year.
That is why I asked my hon. friend what would be the cost of drilling the city regiments this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The training of the city regiments and the semi-city regiments will absorb $742,000. The other items 'are in reference to the permanent force and are as follows: Transport of the permanent force to and from camps, $17,000; rations of the permanent force in camps, $57,000; forage far 993 permanent corps horses, $50,000; fuel and lights iat camps, $1,000; engineers fitting up camps, $25,000. I assume that all but the first item of $742,000 relate to the permanent force, but that item is the cost af the drilling of the city and the semi-city corps.
-Sir SAM HUGHES: I regret exceedingly, Mr. Chairman, that the minister has not included the rural corps in the annual training.
Not in that estimate.

I regret to hear the opinion expressed that it is detrimental to the interests of any country to take these men from production. There is not a county in Canada to-day but could produce twice as much-if the people would only -work energetically. I do not regard it as a loss to the community at all to have these men take their annual training in camp. The late leader of the Opposition-and I trust his successor to-day will endorse this policy-expressed the opinion many times in the House that every man-not 43,000 or
80,000	men, but every man-between 18 and 60 years of age should be trained and should be obliged to have his rifle ready, and in rural districts his horse and saddle also, and be prepared to turn out in the defence of his country. That would involve a vastly greater sum that is asked by the minister to-day. But I regret that any difference should be made between the city and the rural corps in regard to annual training. I presume the reason is that the minister is not ready to proceed with the training of the rural corps. II would remind the House that in the great war our rural corps proved to be the backbone of our fighting force. They have always done their duty well and turned out in magnificent numbers, and . have shown themselves second to none.
How many city corps will be sent to the Valcartier Camp for training?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There will be none sent to Valcartier. The Royal Canadian Regiment will train there. The city corps will train at their own headquarters right where they live.

I understand that the Esltimate of $900,000 is for the training of
43,000	men. Has any Estimate been prepared of the cost of training the rural corps?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. The item as it
appeared in the Estimates is $1,500,000, and it included the drilling of the rural corps up to 80 per cent of their full strength. But for the reasons I have given the rural corps will not be able to turn ouit in strength, and rather than have them come forward in very small detachments it was thought advisable to dispense with their training for the present. If we dispense with their training the estimated cost of training the city and the semi-city corps is $953,000. So there would be a balance on hand on -this vote of $545,000.
I assume the Estimate could be reduced by that amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, II would not say
that. It has been sanctioned by His Excellency the Governor General as it is now. But things might develop and in the autumn of the year it might become necessary to train the rural corps. I do not know. For some years past the annual training has always takdn place in June. But I remember, the first camp I attended was in September of 1885, in London, and I think that was the best camp I was ever at. So far the rural corps are not in shape to go to camp, and as the item stands now it can be expended only for the purpose for which it is voted.

I should like to point out that no money -publicly expended is so well distributed among the people of the country as is the money voted under this item. The expenditure for annual drill is distributed among forty or fifty thousand men.
The minister has told us that some of the rural corps may be called out for training in the fall. What are these rural corps? Are they in the province of Quebec, in Ontario, or out West?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If any rural corps in any part of Canada which are at full strength desire to train this year, I think it could be arranged for them. I know that in Western Ontario there are said to be two units fairly well up to strength; it might be possible for these to train. Of course, it depends largely on the decision of the officers. It would be much better to have the regular brigade camps, but this year I do not think it is possible to have them.
Has the minister anything before him to enable him to say that more than two rural corps will be called out for training in the fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The information was at hand and was examined by Militia Council between two and three weeks ago. I am only speaking from recollection as to my part of Western Ontario when I refer to the only two that I know of. It may be that there are others in other parts of the country. But the information which has come to us generally from all parts of Canada is to the effect that we could not have a satisfactory camp of rural corps this year. That is the opinion of officers commanding the rural corps as well as of officers commanding military districts. In these circumstances it would be idle for us to go ahead with the proposal.
What would be the approximate cost of training these two rural corps?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know just what it would cost, but it would cost proportionately a little more to train two than to train a dozen.
Then I understand that the minister has before him information to the effect that 43,000 men belonging to city corps will be trained and that two Ontario rural corps will also be trained?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not say that. I
said there were two that I thought were sufficiently near full strength to train. I did not say there was a probability that these would be trained; there is a possibility.

There is a possibility that they will be trained, and a probability that they will not. So, leaving these rural units out of consideration, I may point out that the minister intends this year to train
43,000	men. The cost of that training will be 8950,000; yet the minister asks the committee to-night for 81,500,000. I do not think that the position taken by the minister is reasonable; he should not ask the committee to vote $600,000 more than he needs, especially if he is sincere, as I believe he is, in his declaration oif willingness to economize.

How many of the 600,000 men who were enlisted served in the firing line in France?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid I have not that information; I did not know that the question would arise on this item. The matter is one which might more properly come up under the Demobilization vote. I have a statement of those who have been returned from overseas since 'the Armistice; that is the nearest I can come to it just now.
How many were returned since the Armistice?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The number is 273,565.

I understand that not more than 350,000 of these 600,000 men have served in France. The minister has made a great display of the sacrifices and the great effort put forth by the Dominion of Canada in recruiting 600,000 men of whom less than 350,000 -went to the front. He has pointed out that this is a great record for any nation. I should like to know if it was necessary in other nations 'to recruit twelve men in order that seven might go to the front, or if it was necessary to retain five in the country fpr every seven who got to the front -as fighting men in the -armies.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think I have the figures as to ho-w many served either in England or in France. The statement which was furnished to the House of Commons on the 10th March and which appears in Hansard of that date reads as follows:
(a) Grand total recruited in Canada for Canadian Expeditionary Force during the war up

to 31st December, 1918, (exclusive of those enlisted for Naval Service, Royal Air Force, Imperial Mechanical Transport, Inland Water Transport, and exclusive of British and Allied reservists) 591,472 ; (b) Enlisted in England up to 31st December, 1918, 1,733 ; (c) Enlisted in Canada for overseas service other than Canadian Expeditionary Force, 21,169 ;	(d) British and Allied Reservists exclusive of (c)) 14,590. Total 628,964.
That does not show how many of these men served in England or France.
I understand -a statement was made to some -committee of the House giving the number of men who had actually served in France.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sure the figures are on Hansard somewhere. I know the figures have been furnished.
Mr. COPP; The Committee on Re-establishment last year, I think, put the figure at 235,000.
Would the minister say whether o-uit of .the 628,000, only 235,000 saw active service?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have never heard that statement. I think that figure is incorrect.
What i-s the correct figure?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It has been furnished to the Hou-s-e. I "would h-ave thought this question would coime up on the Demobilization vote, or I would have been prepared with the figures. This is not a matter which -affects the militia vote.
The Demobilization vote includes anything that can possibly be included in -any vote.

The item before the committee at the present time is item No. 92 referring to annual drill. I have not up to the present interfered with the discussion, but I think it is getting entirely aw-a-y from the item actually before the committee.

I move that the chairman do now leave the Chair.
Motion negatived.

The Minister of Militia stated that some- six hundred odd thousand men were enlisted, and when you, Sir, interrupted me I was -asking him how many had seen active service. I should like to have -an answer to that question.
I would again call the -attention of the hon. -member to the fact that his question has no relation to the item under discussion and I must, therefore, rule his question out of order.
I-s it in order to rule my question out of order after permitting -the minister to make a statement as to the number of men who have seen active service?
Would the minister state to the committee the period of annual training for the various city battalions? How long will that drill last?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It -amounts to twelve days' pay for two drills -a day; it is really twenty four drills for twelve days' pay.
What is the average co-s-t per man?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: $1.40 per day for city corps' privates.
What is the average cost per officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I could not give the -average, but I -can give the officers' -pay: lieutenant-colonel, $8; major, $6.50; captain, $5.50; lieutenant, $4; paymaster, $4.75; quartermaster, $4.75; -medical officer, $4.75; chaplain, $6; warrant officer, $2.80; quartermaster sergeant, $2.75; staff sergeant-, $2.30; sergeant, $2; corporal, $1.70; -bugler, $1.50; bandsman, $1.50; private $1.40.
Are there officers ranking above the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not in the militia.
What about officers who were overseas and attained the rank of full coloneil, or brigadier-general, or major-general, and "who have reverted to the militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They retain the brevet
rank overseas, but in the militia the high est rank is lieutenant-colonel. They are entitled to the brevet rank they attained overseas.

Is it the intention of the department to do what is done in France, I understand, namely, to reform the militia list; that is, to give back to each officer the rank to which he is entitled, reducing him in rank although he might have held a superior rank during the war? Is suich a process going to take place as regards our militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That process has taken place in many cases. If a man got a higher rank in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, he is entitled to retain that rank on his brevet rank only. On going back to the militia he will revert to his former rank. That has occurred in the militia and also in the permanent force.

How would the
minister explain the position of an officer who had held the rank'of major at the front and who is now a sergeant in the permanent force?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In the case put to me
by my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) the man would have the right to elect whether he would revert to his former rank in the permanent force or whether he would retire on pension. If he had been ten years in the service he would be entitled to retire on pension; if he had been less than ten years in the service he would be entitled to retire and obtain a gratuity depending on his length of service.
Has the minister appointed any honorary colonels since he took charge of the department, and if so, how many?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have not been able to find a victim yet.

I think the minister ought to agree now to reduce this item by at least $500,000. He has stated that he will very probably not need that extra half million. He has voted down the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition, but according to his own statement the item could be reduced by half a million dollars. That should be done. It would be a step in the right direction. I feel some hesitation in giving this Government any more money than they require because I am not certain how they will use it. I was very much astonished this morning to find that a Bureau of Information is being conducted in this city, and that the money to pay for it is being taken out of the demobilization vote passed last year. I was also shocked to discover a few days ago that we are running a news agency in the city of New York, which it is estimated will cost $30,000 for the year, which amount is also being taken, by Order in Council, out of the demobilization vote of last year. I think therefore it is very unsafe to give to this Government any more money than is actually required, and I would appeal to the minister to agree to at least $500,000 of this amount being struck out without any motion being made to that effect.

The minister said he
would not reduce this amount because he had been authorized by the Governor in Council to introduce a resolution for $1,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I did not give that as a reason for not reducing the item.

The minister's contention would be sound if the proposal was to increase the item, but he is irerfeetly at liberty to reduce it, so his argument is no argument at all from the constitutional point of view, nor from the political point of view. Are we the representatives of the people?
No.
Hear, hear.
I am gratified, Mr. Chairman, after having sat in Ottawa for four months 'this session, that we have at least convinced hon. gentlemen opposite that they are not the representatives of the people.
They have just admitted it.

We have their own admission on Hansard. If they do not represent the people, whom do they represent?
Mr. CAiSGRAIN: Themselves.
The trusts.

My hon. friend from Brantford, in the course of the discussion this evening, talked about the thundering cannon. I may not be the thundering Cannon, but I would just as soon 'be what I am as a screeching plough. And when the hon. gentleman says that he is entitled to speak before this committee because he is the one who pays the taxes, I answer that he does not pay the taxes of this country. If he paid the taxes of this country as he should pay them, the Budget and the Estimates brought down by this Government would be very different. The Budget would not have been prepared and dictated by the manufacturers but by the common people of this country. The time has come, Mr. Chairman, for both the Government and the Opposition to fight in the open, and I will not permit any member of this House, whether he represents Brantford or any other constituency, whether he be- a millionaire like the hon. member for Brantford or a poor man like myself, to suggest to this committee, composed of intelligent men, on this side of the House at least, that because he pays taxes we have no taxes to pay. We know very well that gentlemen on the other side of the House do their very best not to pay the taxes, at least those who belong to the class my hon. friend from Brantford belongs to. I want to have a fair and square fight, and I will not stand for any argument of the kind brought forward by my hon. friend from Brantford.

I say that on the minister's own admission, he only needs for drill halls this year $950,000, not a cent more. We have had enough waste and enough money squandered in Canada. It is time to stop. Money was wasted by hon. gentlemen opposite. Money was squandered by their friends-
Explain.

It is useless to explain; you would not understand. When money was to be wasted or squandered the Whip on the other side of the House did not need to crack his whip for the docile troop of Government supporters would come in and vote the money. These gentlemen may have a majority in Parliament, but they have no following in the country. We have been told that this Government would come out with a programme. Where is their programme? It was to be elaborated at a caucus. When will the caucus be held? Some papers say Monday, others Tuesday, some say this week, others next week. These are the gentlemen who are running Canada. They talk about how great and big this country will become, and they have not even a programme. I heard some one bellow. Will he please speak like a human being.
I asked the hon. gentleman to get down to the subject.
I am corning to the subject and quickly enough. These gentlemen are asking that they be given $600,000 more than they need. What for?
Graft,

Who is going to get that $600,000 Friends of the Government-if there are any left? Are we going to give it to newspaper men to write articles in the United States to tell us what a great man the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) is. Are we going to vote $600,000 more than is required by the Government for drill halls, so that we can have it drilled into our minds that the President of the Privy Council is a great man? During the war, follies were committed. This Government would come before the House and say: "We need so much money and it will be used to save the British Empire." The money was always voted. But now the war is over, and these gentlemen will get exactly w7hat they need and not a cent more. I do not think the minister takes a reasonable stand before this committee when he admits that he only needs $950,000 and yet asks Parliament to vote'him $1,500,000.
